We rephrased our objectives to a single sentence that follows the recommended guidance in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and avoids pre‐empting the findings of the review. We amended the exclusion criteria to exclude cardiac rehabilitation, as it has a particular focus on exercise with some education support. We amended the inclusion criteria to state that clinical service interventions must be multicomponent and involve a multidisciplinary approach to be eligible. Multicomponent and multidisciplinary approach means patients are provided with comprehensive care which meets the definition of clinical service organisations for AF. For the outcome thromboembolic complications, we refined the definition to include stroke and/or TIA instead of stroke and TIA to ensure we captured and included all relevant thromboembolic complications. We changed the definition of all‐cause hospitalisation to include only hospital admissions (i.e. not AF‐related emergency department visits), as an emergency department visit may not necessarily lead to an admission. We did not include Scopus as a bibliographic database, as PubMed and MEDLINE content are a subset of Scopus and should have captured all the relevant articles, in addition to Embase. We calculated and reported the number needed to treat for all‐cause mortality, all‐cause hospitalisation, cardiovascular mortality, thromboembolic complications, and major cerebrovascular bleeding events to ensure the results are interpretable by governmental agencies and stakeholders. We planned to use summary information (log hazard ratio and variance) from the included studies to calculate time‐to‐event data for all‐cause or cardiovascular mortality ( Higgins 2023a ). However, these were not reported in the included studies. For cross‐over RCTs, we planned to take all measurements from intervention E periods and all measurements from intervention C periods and analyse these as if the trial were a parallel‐group trial of E versus C. Whilst this approach generates a unit of analysis issue, it is conservative and less serious than other types of unit of analysis issues, as it underweights rather than overweights studies. However, no cross‐over RCTs were included in the review. We planned to assess for potential publication bias using funnel plots. However, this was precluded by an insufficient number of studies (< 10). We deleted the following planned subgroup analyses to reduce the risk of type I error: people who underwent AF catheter ablation versus people on medical treatment alone; and people with paroxysmal AF versus non‐paroxysmal AF. Had we found definitive evidence of heterogeneity (I² > 50%), we planned to explore potential reasons for differences by conducting the subgroup analyses listed below and meta‐regression ( Normand 1999 ). However, this was precluded by insufficient studies. Age (more than 65 years versus under 65 years). Sex (women versus men). History of heart failure. People with a CHA 2 DS 2 ‐VASc score of 2 or greater versus people with a score of 0 to 1. Comparison of type of intervention (case management versus multidisciplinary versus integrated care versus eHealth models). documents.title: HIV and cardiovascular diseases: a systematic review and comparative risk assessment study.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: People living with HIV (PLWH) face a significantly elevated risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). This study aims to quantify temporal trends in HIV-attributable CVD burden at global, regional and national levels using a comparative risk assessment framework.
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase and MEDLINE for cohort studies from inception to 28 October 2024, assessing HIV infection and CVD risk. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) for total and subtype-specific CVDs were estimated using random-effects meta-analysis. Based on pooled RRs and HIV prevalence data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study, we calculated population attributable fractions (PAFs) from 1990 to 2011. These PAFs were applied to GBD disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) to estimate the age-standardised DALYs rate (ASDRs) of CVDs attributable to HIV by sex, region and year between 2000 and 2021.
FINDINGS: 35 cohort studies with 199 effect estimates were included. HIV infection was associated with increased risk of total CVDs (RR=1.38), stroke (1.90), ischaemic stroke (1.31), haemorrhagic stroke (2.04), ischaemic heart disease (1.72), myocardial infarction (1.60), heart failure (1.71), peripheral vascular disease (1.19) and cardiac arrest (2.58). Subgroup analyses showed higher ischaemic stroke risk in females and increased CVD risk among PLWH with low CD4+ or high viral load. From 1990 to 2011, the global PAF for total CVDs attributable to HIV rose from 0.0814% to 0.2244%. Global ASDR attributable to HIV nearly tripled, increasing from 3.45 to 9.26 per 100 000 population between 2000 and 2021, with stroke and ischaemic heart disease contributing most. The burden was highest in low-Sociodemographic Index regions, particularly southern Africa; in 2021, Lesotho and Eswatini had the highest ASDRs.
INTERPRETATION: HIV-attributable CVD burden has risen substantially over the past two decades, with marked concentration in the African Region. Integrating CVD screening and management into HIV care is urgently needed in high-prevalence settings.

Yet, global evidence on HIV-attributable CVD burden across different regions and subtypes remains limited. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This study provides comprehensive estimates of HIV-related risks for major CVD outcomes and quantifies global, regional and national burdens. We found substantially increased CVD risks among PLWH and a threefold increase in HIV-attributable CVD burden from 2000 to 2021, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY Our findings highlight the urgent need to integrate CVD prevention and management into HIV care programmes, especially in high-risk countries. The study provides an updated evidence base for guiding resource allocation and global health policy on dual HIV-CVD epidemics. Introduction Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally. 1 Over the past three decades, the burden of CVDs has increased substantially, driven by population ageing, changing lifestyle patterns and the rising prevalence of metabolic and behavioural risk factors. 2 3 In parallel, advances in combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) and its widespread availability have transformed HIV infection from a fatal illness into a chronic, manageable condition, resulting in substantial gains in survival and life expectancy for people living with HIV (PLWH). 4 5 As acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS)-related mortality has declined, the clinical profile of HIV has broadened, with non-communicable diseases, particularly CVDs, now contributing an increasing share of morbidity and mortality among PLWH. 6 Numerous epidemiological studies have shown that PLWH experience a substantially elevated risk of CVD events, including myocardial infarction, stroke and heart failure, compared with individuals without HIV, even after achieving sustained viral suppression. 7–9 In some cohorts, HIV infection has also been associated with increased risks of peripheral vascular disease and aortic aneurysm. 10 11 Notably, CVDs now account for an estimated 4.6% of all deaths among PLWH globally, and more than 5% of deaths in Asian cohorts. 12 13 This elevated risk reflects a multifactorial interplay between chronic immune activation, systemic inflammation and ART-related metabolic effect. 14 HIV is known to promote endothelial dysfunction and arterial inflammation, while several ART regimens, particularly older-generation protease inhibitors and thymidine analogues, have been implicated in dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance and lipodystrophy. 6 15 Histopathological and imaging studies have provided further evidence of early vascular ageing, subclinical atherosclerosis and myocardial remodelling in PLWH, even in the absence of overt clinical disease. 16 17 However, the modifying effects of immune status, viral load and ART exposure on cardiovascular risk remain inconsistent and need further comprehensive exploration. Despite the growing recognition of these risks, global estimates of HIV-attributable CVD burden remain limited. Most existing studies have focused on a narrow range of outcomes, primarily myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke, and have been conducted in high-income settings, limiting their generalisability to low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), where nearly 80% of PLWH reside. 9 18 19 In one of the few global assessments to date, a 2018 study estimated that HIV contributed to 2.6 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) of CVDs, with the highest burden observed in sub-Saharan Africa and the Asia-Pacific region. 7 However, that study did not provide stratified estimates by Sociodemographic Index (SDI), nor did it incorporate more recent epidemiological evidence or the full spectrum of cardiovascular outcomes now recognised to be associated with HIV. Comprehensive and up-to-date estimates of HIV-attributable CVD burden are needed to inform the integration of cardiovascular care into chronic HIV management, particularly in regions with high dual burdens of HIV and CVDs. In this study, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the risk ratios (RRs) of major cardiovascular outcomes associated with HIV infection. We then applied a comparative risk assessment framework using data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study to estimate the global, regional and national burden of HIV-attributable CVDs. Specifically, we aimed to: (1) quantify the RRs of major CVD outcomes in PLWH compared with HIV-negative individuals; (2) estimate the population attributable fraction (PAF) of CVDs attributable to HIV, stratified by sex, SDI quintile, WHO region and country between 1990 and 2011; and (3) assess temporal trends in age-standardised DALY rates (ASDRs) for HIV-attributable CVDs at global, regional and national levels from 2000 to 2021. Methods Study design and analytic framework We conducted a comparative risk assessment to estimate the global burden of CVDs attributable to HIV infection. The analysis was based on three sequential steps ( figure 1 ). First, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify the RRs of CVD outcomes in PLWH compared with HIV-negative individuals, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines. 20 21 The study protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (registration number: CRD420251069714); Second, we estimated PAFs for HIV-associated CVD outcomes by combining the pooled RRs from the meta-analysis with HIV prevalence data obtained from the GBD 2021 study for the period 1990–2011. Third, we applied a 10-year exposure-outcome lag, consistent with prior GBD comparative risk assessments and the follow-up durations reported in previous HIV-CVD cohort studies, 22–24 to reflect the delayed effects of chronic HIV infection on cardiovascular pathogenesis, whereby prolonged immune activation and endothelial dysfunction accumulate over several years before clinically manifest CVD outcomes. 25 The resulting PAFs were then applied to GBD estimates of CVD DALYs to derive HIV-attributable ASDRs from 2000 to 2021, disaggregated by sex, SDI quintile, WHO region and country. Systematic review and meta-analysis Search strategy and selection criteria Our literature identification comprised two steps: (1) an updated electronic database search and (2) a manual screening of reference lists from relevant prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses have previously examined the association between HIV infection and incident CVDs. We first reviewed the search periods of these prior studies and identified that while some recent reviews extended beyond 2020 and others ended earlier, most CVD outcomes had already been well covered by studies up to 2020. 26–34 Building on this, we conducted an updated and comprehensive literature search in PubMed, Embase and MEDLINE to identify cohort studies published between 1 January 2020 and 28 October 2024 that investigated the associations between HIV infection and the risk of CVDs. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms related to HIV (eg, “HIV”, “AIDS”, “human immunodeficiency virus”) and CVDs (eg, “cardiovascular disease”, “myocardial infarction”, “stroke”, “heart failure”). No restrictions were applied regarding language or geographic region. Eligible studies were restricted to full-text, peer-reviewed journal articles. To ensure completeness, we also manually screened the reference lists of included articles and relevant prior reviews. The full search strategy is provided in online supplemental table S1 . 10.1136/bmjgh-2025-022324.supp1 Supplementary data Studies were eligible for inclusion if they: (1) used a cohort design; (2) reported the association between HIV infection and the risk of CVD morbidity or mortality; and (3) provided effect estimates as RRs, HRs or ORs with 95% CIs. Eligible CVD outcomes included both composite and specific endpoints, including stroke, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, cerebral aneurysm, ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, cardiac arrest, aortic aneurysm, peripheral vascular disease, sudden cardiac death, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension and coronary heart disease. When multiple publications reported findings from the same cohort population, the one with the most comprehensive data or the largest sample size was retained. However, if distinct CVD subtypes were reported across publications from the same cohort, each was included. We excluded studies that focused solely on individuals with pre-existing CVDs or on CVD-related rehospitalisation, as well as those without a clearly defined HIV exposure group. Screening, data extraction and quality assessment Two reviewers (ZL and CZ) independently screened the titles and abstracts of all retrieved articles, followed by full-text screening of potentially eligible studies. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. Data extraction was independently performed by two investigators (TH and RL) using a predefined and standardised data collection form, and verified by a third investigator (ZL) to ensure accuracy and consistency. The extracted information included: title, first author, publication year, investigation year, study location, WHO region (African Region (AFR), Region of the Americas (AMR), South-East Asian Region (SEAR), European Region (EUR), Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) and Western Pacific Region (WPR)), SDI region (high, high-middle, middle, low-middle and low, classified according to the study-year SDI values based on the reference quantiles defined in GBD 2021), sample sources (community-based, health facility-based or combined), sample size, proportion of female participants, participant age (range, mean or median), measurement of HIV, measurement of CVDs and its subtypes, risk estimates (RR, HR or OR), and corresponding 95% CIs, prioritising fully adjusted estimates when multiple models were reported. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), which assigns a maximum of nine stars across three domains: selection of participants, comparability of study groups and ascertainment of outcomes/exposures. 35 Studies were categorised as having good quality (NOS score ≥7), fair quality (score 4–6) or poor quality (score <4). Quality assessment was independently conducted by two reviewers (ZL and TH), with disagreements resolved by consensus. Data sources for HIV prevalence and cardiovascular burden Data on HIV prevalence and DALYs for CVDs were obtained from the GBD 2021 study, coordinated by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation. 36 HIV prevalence was extracted for the period 1990–2011. With a 10-year exposure-outcome lag, DALYs were extracted for the period 2000–2021, for both overall CVDs and six CVD subtypes defined in the GBD database, namely ischaemic heart disease, stroke, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension. Given that most cohorts included individuals aged 18 years and older, the data were extracted by 5-year age intervals (from 20 to 24 to 95+ years). These data were also stratified by sex, SDI region, WHO region and country. Statistical analysis Meta-analysis of effect estimates Included studies reported effect estimates in the forms of HRs, RRs and ORs, along with their 95% CIs. Given the low incidence of CVD events (<5%) among HIV-negative comparator groups in most cohorts, RRs and HRs were considered numerically equivalent and were pooled directly. 37 38 For studies reporting ORs, we applied a standard transformation to approximate RRs 39 using the following formula: R R i j = O R i j 1 - P i + ( P i × O R i j ) S E l n ⁡ ( R R i j ) = S E l n ⁡ ( O R i j ) = l n ⁡ ( U C i j ) - l n ⁡ ( L C i j ) 3 . 92 R R 95 % C I , i j = e l n ⁡ ( R R i j ) ± 1.96 × S E l n ⁡ ( R R i j ) where O R i j is the point estimate of OR from each study i and data point j; R R i j is the point estimate of RR from each study i and data point j; P i is the study-specific prevalence of outcome among the unexposed group (when not reported, prevalence was obtained from previously published meta-analyses of the corresponding outcome); l n is natural log; S E is standard error; L C i j is lower confidence limit and U C i j is upper confidence limit of 95% CI. We conducted a random-effects meta-analysis with the restricted maximum likelihood estimator to calculate pooled effect estimates for overall CVDs and individual subtypes, where at least two studies were available. When multiple subgroup-specific estimates (eg, for sex) were reported within the same study, they were first meta-analysed using a fixed-effects model to generate a single study-level estimate prior to pooling. 40 Pooled RRs with corresponding 95% CIs were reported. Between-study heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic, with values >50% indicating substantial heterogeneity. 41 Publication bias was evaluated through visual inspection of funnel plots, and asymmetry was tested using Egger’s regression test when at least ten estimates were available (a p<0.05 from Egger’s regression test was considered suggestive of small-study effects). 42 Robustness of pooled estimates was explored using leave-one-out sensitivity analyses. Prespecified subgroup analyses were performed by sex (female vs male), age (<50 vs ≥50 years), sex and age (female, younger (<50 years) vs female, older (≥50 years) vs male, younger (<50 years) vs male, older (≥50 years)), ethnicity (white vs non-white), CD4+cell count (<200 vs 200–499 vs ≥500 cells/mm³), HIV viral load (≥500 vs <500 copies/mL), sampling source (community-based vs health facility-based vs combined), and WHO region (AMR vs EUR vs WPR). Credibility and grading of evidence Each pooled estimate was assessed for credibility by two investigators (ZL and TH) using a five-grade classification system based on the strength and consistency of the evidence. Criteria included statistical significance (p value), 95% CI width, between-study heterogeneity (I²), prediction intervals, small-study effects, excess significance bias and whether the largest contributing study reported a significant effect. Based on these dimensions, evidence was classified as convincing (class I), highly suggestive (class II), suggestive (class III), weak (class IV) or non-significant (class NS), as detailed in online supplemental table S2 . 43 44 Additionally, we assessed the quality of evidence for each pooled estimate using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, categorising them as ‘high’, ‘moderate’, ‘low’ or ‘very low’. 45 According to the GRADE approach, observational studies are initially rated as low-quality evidence. Confidence in the effect estimates may be downgraded based on five criteria: risk of bias, inconsistency among studies, indirectness of the evidence, imprecision and potential publication bias. Conversely, confidence may be upgraded if certain conditions are met, including a large effect size unlikely to be explained by confounders, evidence of a dose-response relationship and no plausible residual confounding that could alter the interpretation of the exposure’s effect. Estimation of HIV-attributable cardiovascular burden To quantify the burden of CVDs attributable to HIV infection, we first calculated the PAF for each outcome using the formula: P A F = P × ( R R - 1 ) P × ( R R - 1 ) + 1 where P is the HIV prevalence and R R is the overall pooled RR for each CVD and its subtype. Estimates were stratified by year, sex, age, WHO region and SDI region. We then applied direct age standardisation using the GBD world standard population as the reference to calculate age-standardised PAFs. 46 To propagate uncertainty, we employed Monte Carlo simulation with 1000 iterations. In each iteration, values were sampled jointly from the beta distribution for HIV prevalence and the log-normal distribution for the pooled RR. The PAF estimates were summarised as the mean and 95% CIs, defined as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the simulated distribution. Next, the HIV-attributable burden of CVDs was then estimated by applying the simulated PAFs to the corresponding DALYs (lagged by 10 years to account for latency between exposure and disease onset) obtained from the GBD 2021 dataset: a t t r i b u t a b l e b u r d e n = P A F × D A L Y s Direct standardisation approach was applied to calculate the ASDRs for individuals aged 20 years and older, using the GBD world standard population as the reference. 46 The same simulation approach was used to propagate uncertainty, generating 1000 estimates of a t t r i b u t a b l e b u r d e n for each stratified group. Final estimates were reported as means with corresponding 95% CIs. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using alternative latency assumptions of 8 and 12 years. For the 8-year lag, PAFs were estimated for 1990–2013 and corresponding ASDRs for 1998–2021, whereas for the 12-year lag, PAFs were estimated for 1990–2009 and corresponding ASDRs for 2002–2021. All statistical analyses were conducted using R, V.4.4.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Statistical tests were two-sided, and p values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Results Study selection and characteristics Based on the reference lists of previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses, we identified 107 records. After excluding 36 irrelevant records, 71 articles underwent full-text assessment. We also identified 8635 bibliographic records through electronic database searches. After removing 349 duplicates and excluding 8178 records based on title and abstract screening, we assessed the full texts of 108 articles. Overall, we assessed 179 full-text articles for eligibility and finally included 35 cohort studies in our systematic review and meta-analysis ( figure 2A ). These studies contributed 199 datapoints on associations between HIV and CVDs. These studies were conducted in five countries: the USA (n=24, 68.57%), Denmark (n=4, 11.43%), China (Taiwan province) (n=3, 8.57%), Canada (n=2, 5.71%) and the UK (n=2, 5.71%) ( figure 2B ). Most included studies were conducted in high SDI regions, with the majority originating from the AMR region (n=26, 74.29%). Of the included studies, 25 were health facility-based (71.43%), nine were community-based (25.71%), and one was conducted in both community and health facility settings (2.86%) ( figure 2C ). The included studies varied substantially in study period (ranging from the mid-1980s to 2020), sample size (from fewer than 2000 to over 18 million participants), and population characteristics. Most studies were published after 2010 (n=33, 94.29%). In terms of effect measures, 28 studies reported HRs (80.00%), six reported RRs (17.14%), and one reported an OR (2.86%). Quality assessment using the NOS criteria indicated that 34 studies (97.14%) were of good methodological quality, while one (2.86%) was of fair quality. Detailed characteristics and quality assessments of the included studies can be found in online supplemental table S3–S5 . Pooled associations between HIV and cardiovascular outcomes As shown in figure 3 , the pooled RR for overall CVDs in PLWH compared with those without HIV was 1.38 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.83; credibility: class IV; GRADE: very low). The associations varied by CVD subtype. For stroke, the pooled RR was 1.90 (95% CI 1.56 to 2.32; class I; low), including both ischaemic stroke (RR=1.31, 95% CI 1.18 to 1.46; class I; low) and haemorrhagic stroke (RR=2.04, 95% CI 1.63 to 2.56; class I; moderate). Significant associations were also found for ischaemic heart disease (RR=1.72, 95% CI 1.40 to 2.13; class II; low), myocardial infarction (RR=1.60, 95% CI 1.36 to 1.87; class II; very low), heart failure (RR=1.71, 95% CI 1.39 to 2.09; class II; very low), peripheral vascular disease (RR=1.19, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.25; class I; low) and cardiac arrest (RR=2.58, 95% CI 2.27 to 2.92; class II; moderate). Among less frequently reported outcomes, increased risks were observed for pulmonary hypertension (RR=1.18, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.34) and atrial fibrillation (RR=1.30, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.70). No statistically significant associations were noted for aortic aneurysm, sudden cardiac death or cerebral aneurysm. The overall certainty of evidence assessed by GRADE ranged from moderate to very low across outcomes, with most estimates rated as low ( online supplemental table S6 ). The funnel plots revealed no evidence of publication bias. Detailed results from the single studies included in the meta-analysis, as well as the forest plot, funnel plot and sensitivity analysis results for each meta-analysis, are provided in online supplemental table S7 . Subgroup analyses revealed several differential patterns in the associations between HIV and CVDs ( online supplemental table S8 ). Subgroup analyses revealed a higher risk of ischaemic stroke in females (RR=1.76, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.52) than in males (RR=1.13, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.28; p for subgroup differences=0.021). No significant sex-based differences were observed for other outcomes. Immunosuppression (CD4+<200 cells/mm³) was strongly associated with increased risk of myocardial infarction (RR=1.83, 95% CI 1.51 to 2.21; p=0.008), heart failure (RR=1.70, 95% CI 1.49 to 1.95; p=0.013), ischaemic stroke (RR=3.20, 95% CI 2.30 to 4.40; p<0.0001), peripheral vascular disease (RR=1.91, 95% CI 1.71 to 2.13; p<0.0001), aortic aneurysm (RR=1.29, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.65; p=0.038), sudden cardiac death (RR=1.57, 95% CI 1.28 to 1.92; p=0.003) and pulmonary hypertension (RR=1.94, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.54; p<0.0001), compared with individuals with preserved immune function (CD4+≥200 cells/mm³). Similarly, high viral load (≥500 copies/mL) was significantly associated with elevated risks of ischaemic stroke (RR=2.24, 95% CI 1.73 to 2.89; p<0.0001), peripheral vascular disease (RR=1.51, 95% CI 1.38 to 1.65; p<0.0001), aortic aneurysm (RR=1.29, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.52; p=0.003), sudden cardiac death (RR=1.70, 95% CI 1.46 to 1.98; p<0.0001) and pulmonary hypertension (RR=1.88, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.42; p=0.0002). For sudden cardiac death, the risk was markedly higher in community-based study (RR=8.15, 95% CI 5.58 to 11.90; p<0.0001) than in health facility-based study, and was also substantially higher in the WPR (RR=8.15, 95% CI 5.58 to 11.90; p<0.0001) compared with the AMR. By sex and age, the higher risks were observed among younger females, for both haemorrhagic stroke (RR=4.32, 95% CI 3.14 to 5.96; p<0.0001) and coronary heart disease (RR=1.31, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.47; p<0.0001). By contrast, no significant subgroup differences were observed across age alone or ethnicity. Burden of CVDs attributable to HIV Global burden of CVDs attributable to HIV Globally, the PAF of HIV-associated CVDs increased from 0.0814% (95% CI 0.0790% to 0.0837%) in 1990 to 0.2244% (0.2201% to 0.2288%) in 2011 ( online supplemental table S9 ). The corresponding ASDR nearly tripled from 3.45 (95% CI 3.42 to 3.48) per 100 000 population in 2000 to 9.26 (95% CI 9.09 to 9.42) in 2021 ( figure 4A and online supplemental table S10 ). The sharpest increase occurred between 2000 and 2010, followed by a period of relative stabilisation from approximately 2010 to 2015, and a subsequent gradual increase thereafter. Among specific CVD subtypes, both the PAFs in 2011 and ASDRs in 2021 were highest for stroke (particularly haemorrhagic stroke) and ischaemic heart disease. In 2011, the global PAFs reached 0.5296% (95% CI 0.5193% to 0.5399%) for stroke and 0.4242% (95% CI 0.4159% to 0.4325%) for ischaemic heart disease, significantly higher than those for ischaemic stroke (0.1832%), atrial fibrillation (0.1773%) and pulmonary hypertension (0.1065%). By 2021, the corresponding ASDRs per 100 000 population were 7.75 (95% CI 7.57 to 7.93) for stroke and 7.94 (95% CI 7.79 to 8.08) for ischaemic heart disease, again markedly surpassing those of other CVDs. Haemorrhagic stroke showed the highest burden among stroke subtypes, with a 2011 PAF of 0.6113% (95% CI 0.5995% to 0.6232%) and a 2021 ASDR of 6.01 (95% CI 5.84 to 6.18) per 100 000 population. In contrast, ASDRs for ischaemic stroke, atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension in 2021 remained low at 0.88, 0.09 and 0.01 per 100 000 population, respectively. Sex-stratified results showed that the relative PAFs were slightly higher in females than in males in 2011, while the ASDR of CVDs attributable to HIV was consistently higher in males (12.70, 95% CI 12.43 to 12.97) than in females (6.35, 95% CI 6.21 to 6.49) in 2021 ( figure 4 , online supplemental table S9, S10 ). Similar trends were observed across CVD subtypes. Regional burden of CVDs attributable to HIV For SDI regions, from 2000 to 2021, ASDR per 100 000 population of HIV-associated CVDs rose from 29.77 (95% CI 29.06 to 30.48) to 41.15 (95% CI 39.80 to 42.49) in low SDI region and from 5.90 (95% CI 5.81 to 5.99) to 17.31 (95% CI 16.91 to 17.72) in low-middle SDI region ( figure 4 , online supplemental table S10 ). By 2021, the ASDR per 100 000 population in low SDI regions remained the highest, particularly for stroke (35.50, 95% CI 34.18 to 36.83), haemorrhagic stroke (29.85, 95% CI 27.99 to 31.71) and ischaemic heart disease (30.43, 95% CI 29.36 to 31.49). Moderate burdens were observed in low-middle SDI and middle SDI regions, while high and high-middle SDI regions reported the lowest ASDRs per 100 000 population of HIV-attributable CVDs at 2.71 (95% CI 2.66 to 2.76) and 2.30 (95% CI 2.25 to 2.35), respectively. These patterns were mirrored in PAFs in 2011, ranging from 0.7028% (95% CI 0.6901% to 0.7154%) in low SDI to 0.0512% (95% CI 0.0464% to 0.0559%) in high-middle SDI ( online supplemental table S9 ). Across WHO regions, a similar divergent trend was observed. The AFR experienced a dramatic rise in ASDR per 100 000 population from 40.68 (95% CI 39.62 to 41.74) in 2000 to 102.18 (95% CI 98.84 to 105.51) in 2021, while most other regions showed either minor increases or stable trends. For example, the ASDR per 100 000 population in SEAR increased from 0.31 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.31) to 4.63 (95% CI 4.53 to 4.74), and AMR from 2.81 (95% CI 2.79 to 2.84) to 5.54 (95% CI 5.45 to 5.63). In contrast, EMR and WPR maintained low levels, reaching only 1.31 (95% CI 1.26 to 1.35) and 1.68 (95% CI 1.60 to 1.75) per 100 000 population, respectively, in 2021. By 2021, AFR remained the most severely affected, with notably high ASDRs per 100 000 population for stroke (99.53 (95% CI 95.91 to 103.14)), haemorrhagic stroke (77.22 (95% CI 72.86 to 81.58)) and ischaemic heart disease (61.51 (95% CI 59.37 to 63.65)). PAFs in 2011 reflected the similar ranking, with AFR reaching 1.7588% (95% CI 1.7381% to 1.7795%) for total CVDs. National burden of CVDs attributable to HIV From 1990 to 2021, national-level HIV-attributable CVD burden demonstrated a clear geographic shift and intensification, particularly in southern Africa ( figure 4 , online supplemental figure S1, S2 ). In 1990, the highest PAFs were observed in Zimbabwe, Uganda, Zambia, Malawi and the United Republic of Tanzania, while by 2000, these countries, especially Uganda, Zimbabwe and Zambia, also ranked among those with the highest ASDRs. However, the epicentre of burden rapidly shifted towards southern Africa in the following decade. By 2011, Eswatini, Lesotho, Botswana, South Africa and Zimbabwe topped the list in PAFs. In 2021, Lesotho, Eswatini, Zimbabwe, Botswana and Zambia reported the highest ASDRs, all exceeding 370 per 100 000 population. Sensitivity analyses using alternative time-lag assumptions (8-year and 12-year lags) showed patterns consistent with the primary 10-year lag analysis ( online supplemental figure S3, table S11 ), with a sustained increasing trend in global ASDRs over time. Across all lag periods, stroke (particularly haemorrhagic stroke) and ischaemic heart disease remained the leading contributors to the HIV-attributable CVD burden, and males consistently exhibited higher ASDRs than females. Discussion Based on 199 effect estimates systematically synthesised from 35 cohort studies, HIV infection was associated with increased risks across multiple CVD outcomes (including total CVDs, stroke, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, cardiac arrest, pulmonary hypertension and atrial fibrillation). The global burden of CVDs attributable to HIV has risen markedly over time. The PAF increased significantly between 1990 and 2011, while the ASDR nearly tripled, from 3.45 to 9.26 per 100 000 population between 2000 and 2021. Among specific CVD types, stroke and ischaemic heart disease contributed most substantially to overall HIV-attributable CVD burden and exhibited the largest increases over time. Marked disparities in burden were observed across sociodemographic strata. The global HIV-attributable CVD burden was higher in males than females and highest in low SDI regions, particularly in the AFR, where the ASDR reached 102.18 per 100 000 population in 2021, far exceeding the global average. These results provide a scientific basis for guiding global and regional public health policy, informing resource allocation and improving clinical management, and highlight the urgent need to integrate CVD prevention and management into comprehensive HIV care strategies. Our study found that PLWH showed significantly increased risks of CVDs. HIV infection was significantly associated with higher risk of CVDs, including total CVDs, stroke, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, cardiac arrest, pulmonary hypertension and atrial fibrillation. The pathophysiological mechanisms underlying this association are multifactorial. Persistent immune activation and chronic inflammation represent hallmark features of HIV infection that continue despite effective ART and contribute significantly to CVD risk. 47 The HIV infection process leads to sustained activation of the immune system, characterised by elevated levels of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and high-sensitivity C reactive protein, which contribute to endothelial dysfunction and vascular damage, key precursors to CVDs. 48 49 Moreover, direct damage of HIV proteins on endothelial function and cholesterol metabolism also contributes to cardiovascular pathology. HIV proteins, such as Tat and Nef, accelerate atherosclerosis by damaging endothelial cells and promoting inflammation. 47 The HIV Tat protein can enter dysfunctional endothelial cells via integrin-mediated pathways, promoting viral replication and vascular injury. 50 The HIV Nef protein contributes to cardiovascular pathology by disrupting cholesterol metabolism and impairing reverse cholesterol transport. 51 Besides, microbial translocation from the gut is another contributor to atherosclerosis, further increasing CVD risk. 49 While ART is essential for viral suppression, it has been associated with significant metabolic abnormalities, including dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance and lipodystrophy, all of which compound CVD risk. 47 52 53 The elevated CVD risk among PLWH underscores the urgent need to develop HIV-specific strategies for CVD risk reduction. Beyond viral suppression, an integrated clinical approach, including early cardiovascular risk screening, comprehensive assessment and tailored interventions incorporated into routine HIV care is important. HIV infection was associated with a sex-specific impact on CVD risk, with females exhibiting a significantly higher risk of ischaemic heart disease compared with males. Such a disproportionate risk among females with HIV reflects a confluence of biological vulnerabilities, including reduced oestradiol (E2) levels, metabolic dysregulation and heightened inflammatory responses and immune activation. 54–56 In our study, PLWH with severely depressed immune function of CD4+<200 cells/mm³ and high viral load had significantly increased risk of CVDs. This finding is biologically plausible and supports the central role of uncontrolled viral replication and advanced immunosuppression in driving chronic immune activation, endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis among PLWH, even in the era of ART. 25 57 Furthermore, PLWH in community settings showed high CVD risk. This emphasises social-contextual drivers beyond medical measures in integrated CVD prevention strategies for HIV care delivery. However, we did not observe significant subgroup differences by age or ethnicity. This may be attributable to sample size limitations or underlying data heterogeneity. Future studies with more detailed stratification are warranted to elucidate the potential modifying effects of demographic factors or treatment-related factors on HIV-associated CVD risk. Between 2000 and 2021, the ASDR of CVDs attributable to HIV nearly tripled, with a sharp increase from 2000 to 2010, followed by a period of relative stabilisation from approximately 2010 to 2015, and a subsequent gradual increase thereafter. This trend likely reflects the widespread expansion of ART, which has significantly prolonged life expectancy among PLWH. As PLWH increasingly survive into older age, they become more susceptible to age-related chronic conditions, particularly CVDs, which now represent a growing contributor to long-term morbidity and disability in this population. 53 The most pronounced increases in ASDRs were observed for stroke, particularly haemorrhagic stroke and ischaemic heart disease, substantially exceeding those for atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension and other CVD subtypes. Sex-stratified analyses further revealed distinct patterns between PAF and CVD burden. While PAFs were slightly higher among females than males in 2011, the ASDRs of CVDs attributable to HIV remained consistently higher in males than in females in 2021. This apparent divergence likely reflects differences in baseline cardiovascular risk and background CVD burden between sexes, whereby males generally experience higher absolute CVD rates, while females may exhibit a relatively stronger proportional impact of HIV on cardiovascular risk. 56 58 Together, these findings highlight the increasing importance of sex-specific and disease-specific strategies for cardiovascular prevention and management among ageing PLWH. The ASDR of CVDs attributable to HIV varied greatly across regions and nations, with particularly severe burdens observed in low SDI regions, especially in the AFR. Similarly elevated burdens were seen in low-middle and middle SDI regions. In contrast, high SDI regions exhibited relatively low ASDRs of CVDs attributable to HIV, with the burden showing signs of stabilisation. These disparities likely reflect underlying socioeconomic inequities and weak health systems, which limit access to high-quality healthcare and preventative interventions. 59 60 Regionally, the AFR was most affected, with the ASDR of CVDs attributable to HIV reaching 102.18 per 100 000 in 2021, far higher than the global average. Within AFR, stroke, ischaemic heart disease and haemorrhagic stroke account for the largest shares of the CVD burden attributable to HIV. Similar, though less severe, patterns are evident in the SEAR and AMR regions. Although the burdens in the EMR, EUR and WPR regions remained comparatively lower, recent upward trends suggest the need for continued surveillance and prevention efforts. Shifts in burden rankings at the national level further reflect the evolving influence of epidemic control efforts, economic development and health system performance. These findings have important implications for shaping regional policies, updating clinical guidelines and informing equitable resource allocation. To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive and up-to-date study to systematically evaluate the risk and burden of CVDs, including its main subtypes, among PLWH, using the most recent and comprehensive evidence. Second, this study further explored the association of demographic factors, immune function and viral load with CVD risk among PLWH, highlighting gender differences and HIV-specific mechanisms underlying CVDs in HIV-infected people. Third, this study combined the epidemiological measure PAF and disease burden measure ASDR to complement each other and comprehensively quantify the burden of CVDs attributable to HIV. Fourth, this study revealed the spatial and temporal trends in the burden of CVDs attributable to HIV across different regions from 2000 to 2021, providing valuable insights for targeted public health interventions and resource allocation. This study has several limitations. First, most of the included studies originated from high-income countries, with limited representation from LMICs, potentially limiting the global generalisability of the findings. Second, heterogeneity in study design, follow-up time and covariate adjustment across the included studies may influence the stability and interpretability of the meta-analysis results. Third, although subgroup analyses suggested between-subgroup differences in HIV-associated cardiovascular risks, pooled RRs were applied in the burden estimation to ensure stability and comparability, which may have masked effect modification at finer population levels. Fourth, most studies relied on baseline measurements of immune function and viral load, failing to account for their dynamic nature over time, which may have limited the ability to capture their time-varying effects on cardiovascular risk. Fifth, detailed data on ART regimens, treatment adherence and drug-related adverse effects were lacking, limiting a more detailed understanding of the role of treatment-related factors in cardiovascular risk. In addition, estimates of national and regional disease burden from the GBD study may be subject to systematic bias due to variations in the completeness and quality of medical records and reporting systems. Future research should expand data collection from low-income countries, incorporate more refined analyses of treatment-related factors and validate findings through prospective cohort studies with more detailed subgroup stratification. Conclusions PLWH show increased risks of CVDs and their various subtypes. The burden of CVDs attributable to HIV has grown over time, with the PAF rising significantly between 1990 and 2011, and the ASDR nearly tripling from 2000 to 2021. Substantial regional disparities exist in the global burden of HIV-related CVDs, with the highest burden observed in lower SDI regions, particularly in the AFR. These findings have important policy implications, underscoring the need for tailored cardiovascular risk stratification and treatment strategies within people with HIV, especially in low-income regions where CVDs among PLWH remain highly prevalent. documents.title: Impact of catheter ablation timing according to duration of atrial fibrillation history on arrhythmia recurrences and clinical outcomes: a meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
AIMS: Catheter ablation is a well-established treatment for symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (PAF) or persistent atrial fibrillation (PsAF) refractory to antiarrhythmic agents, and current guidelines have also upgraded its role as a first-line option for recurrent PAF. However, the optimal timing to maximize rhythm outcomes remains uncertain. To address this gap, the present study sought to investigate the association between diagnosis-to-ablation time (DAT) and age-stratified atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence and clinical outcomes.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Medline, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched through 18 February 2025. Triple-independent selection, extraction, and quality assessment were conducted, with evidence pooled via random-effects meta-analyses. Among the 28 studies (41 431 participants) with a median 24-month follow-up, early ablation (DAT ≤ 1 year) significantly reduced AF recurrence compared to delayed ablation [hazard ratio (HR) 0.65, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.59-0.73]. The benefit of early ablation was consistent for both PAF (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.67-0.77) and PsAF (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.61-0.81). Age-stratified analysis revealed that this effect was significant regardless of age, with the greatest risk reduction observed in individuals ≤ 55 years (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34-0.71). Early ablation was also associated with a reduced risk of repeat ablation, new cardioversion, and cardiovascular hospitalization compared to delayed ablation. Higher CHA₂DS₂-VASc scores, heart failure prevalence, and lower mean left ventricular ejection fraction were associated with greater benefits from early ablation.
CONCLUSION: Early catheter ablation within 1 year of AF diagnosis is associated with a lower risk of recurrence in both PAF and PsAF, with the strongest association observed in patients ≤ 55 years.
documents.conclusions: Early catheter ablation within 1 year of AF diagnosis is associated with a lower risk of recurrence in both PAF and PsAF, with the strongest association observed in patients ≤ 55 years.

Abstract Aims Catheter ablation is a well-established treatment for symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (PAF) or persistent atrial fibrillation (PsAF) refractory to antiarrhythmic agents, and current guidelines have also upgraded its role as a first-line option for recurrent PAF. However, the optimal timing to maximize rhythm outcomes remains uncertain. To address this gap, the present study sought to investigate the association between diagnosis-to-ablation time (DAT) and age-stratified atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence and clinical outcomes. Methods and results Medline, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched through 18 February 2025. Triple-independent selection, extraction, and quality assessment were conducted, with evidence pooled via random-effects meta-analyses. Among the 28 studies (41 431 participants) with a median 24-month follow-up, early ablation (DAT ≤ 1 year) significantly reduced AF recurrence compared to delayed ablation [hazard ratio (HR) 0.65, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.59–0.73]. The benefit of early ablation was consistent for both PAF (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.67–0.77) and PsAF (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.61–0.81). Age-stratified analysis revealed that this effect was significant regardless of age, with the greatest risk reduction observed in individuals ≤ 55 years (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34–0.71). Early ablation was also associated with a reduced risk of repeat ablation, new cardioversion, and cardiovascular hospitalization compared to delayed ablation. Higher CHA₂DS₂-VASc scores, heart failure prevalence, and lower mean left ventricular ejection fraction were associated with greater benefits from early ablation. Conclusion Early catheter ablation within 1 year of AF diagnosis is associated with a lower risk of recurrence in both PAF and PsAF, with the strongest association observed in patients ≤ 55 years. the most prevalent cardiac arrhythmia and a major determinant of morbidity and mortality. 1–5 Its incidence is projected to rise significantly in the coming years, imposing a substantial economic and logistical burden on healthcare systems. 6 Despite advancements in management, optimizing rhythm control strategies remains a persistent challenge. 7 , 8 Early therapeutic intervention is considered beneficial, as AF induces progressive atrial fibrosis, a key driver of atrial remodelling that is closely linked to disease perpetuation. 9 , 10 As structural remodelling advances, the efficacy of rhythm control therapies declines, underscoring the critical importance of timely intervention. 11 Emerging evidence suggests that catheter ablation for AF confers superior efficacy in maintaining freedom from atrial arrhythmia recurrence and alleviating AF-related symptoms compared to antiarrhythmic drug (AAD) therapy, particularly in patients with paroxysmal AF (PAF). 12–16 Moreover, the adoption of catheter ablation as first-line treatment in PAF has been associated with a reduced likelihood of progression to persistent AF (PsAF) when compared to AAD, further supporting its role as a preferred therapeutic approach. 17 , 18 However, a closer examination of the inclusion criteria in these randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reveals that patient selection was largely limited to those with a prolonged history of AF, typically exceeding 6 months, and documented recurrent episodes. 13–20 Although AF frequency and burden were reported differently across studies, the overall burden was substantial, with a considerable proportion of participants having previously undergone cardioversion. Importantly, these trials did not encompass individuals presenting with an initial episode of AF, thereby limiting the applicability of their findings to early-stage disease and leaving the potential benefits of catheter ablation in newly diagnosed patients largely unexplored. This gap in evidence raises critical questions regarding the optimal timing of ablation relative to timing of AF diagnosis. While current guidelines support early intervention in selected patients, long-term data on the efficacy and safety of an early ablation strategy in real-world clinical practice remain limited. Additionally, whether the benefits of early intervention extend uniformly across different age groups remains an area of ongoing debate. Given these uncertainties, the present study aimed to evaluate the impact of diagnosis-to-ablation time (DAT) on age-stratified AF recurrence and associated clinical outcomes. Material and methods This study was conducted in accordance with the methodological principles set forth in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews, 21 with its reporting aligned with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. 22 The protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Network (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/BMJYC) and was followed without modifications. Search strategy The search strategy was developed by two researchers (P.K. and N.F.), while a comprehensive and independent literature search was conducted by three researchers across MEDLINE (via PubMed), Scopus, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, from inception to 18 February 2025. No restrictions were imposed regarding date, language, publication status, or year. The search strings incorporated both free-text and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, including atrial fibrillation, ablation, and diagnosis-to-ablation time. To enhance the breadth of the search, additional sources were explored, including manual searches of clinicaltrials.gov , the Epistemonikos database, and Google Scholar. Additionally, backward and forward citation tracking was performed using the citationchaser R package. 23 The complete search strategy is detailed in Supplementary material online , Tables S1 – S3 . Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria Eligible studies included RCTs and observational studies that examined the relationship between DAT and post-ablation outcomes in adults (≥18 years) with AF. Exclusion criteria Studies with the following characteristics were excluded: (i) case reports, case series, and narrative reviews; (ii) editorials, letters, commentaries, and expert opinions; (iii) clinical practice guidelines, conference abstracts, study protocols, and dissertations; and (iv) cross-sectional studies, case-control studies, and crossover trials. Outcomes The primary endpoint of the meta-analysis was the comparative risk of AF recurrence between individuals undergoing early vs. late referral for first-time AF catheter ablation. Secondary outcomes included post-ablation cardioversion, repeat ablation, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, cardiovascular hospitalization, and serious periprocedural adverse events, as defined in the original studies. Early ablation was classified as a DAT of ≤1 year, while late ablation was defined as a DAT exceeding 1 year. This threshold was chosen based on its widespread use in primary literature and the findings of the only available RCT, which reported no significant difference in AF recurrence between ablation at 1 month and 12 months. 24 Study selection In the initial screening phase, three authors independently assessed the titles and abstracts of all records retrieved through the predefined search strategy. To maximize the sensitivity of study selection, no studies were excluded solely based on discrepancies at this stage. Full-text evaluations were then conducted independently by the same three investigators. Any disagreements were adjudicated through consensus or, when necessary, resolved in consultation with a senior author. The screening process was facilitated by Abstrackr, 25 while Mendeley was employed for reference management. Data extraction A structured data extraction form was developed and refined through a pilot phase involving a subset of four studies. Following iterative training and calibration exercises, a standardized form was finalized to ensure consistency and accuracy. Data extraction was conducted independently by three investigators, with discrepancies adjudicated through consensus or, when necessary, consultation with a senior author. For each included study, extracted variables encompassed two broad domains: (i) study-specific details—study design, country, total number of patients with AF, AF subtype, type of catheter ablation, additional ablations, classification as first or repeat ablation, DAT stratification, definition of AF recurrence, blanking period, main inclusion criteria, primary outcome, and follow-up duration and (ii) baseline patient characteristics—group-specific sample size, percentage of male participants, mean age, body mass index (BMI), DAT, CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, left atrial diameter (LAD), history of prior cardioversion, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), AF subtype (paroxysmal or persistent), and comorbidities, including heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity, coronary artery disease, obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), and prior stroke. Where necessary, corresponding authors of the original studies were contacted to obtain additional subgroup-level data that were either missing or not explicitly reported in the published manuscripts. Quality assessment The methodological quality of the included studies was rigorously appraised by two independent reviewers using the Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool, 26 a comprehensive framework designed to evaluate the risk of bias in observational epidemiological research. Any discrepancies in assessment were addressed through deliberation, with unresolved differences adjudicated by a third reviewer when necessary. Data analysis All statistical analyses were conducted using R Statistical Software (v. 4.2). Hazard ratios (HRs) and count data for the predefined endpoints were extracted, with the early ablation group (DAT ≤ 1 year or ≤3 years) serving as the numerator and the late ablation group (DAT > 1 year or >3 years, respectively) as the reference. In instances where HR estimates were not directly reported, binomial data were transformed into HRs using established methodological approaches, 27 consistent with the validated framework applied in our prior meta-analysis on AF-related outcomes. 28 Effect estimates, along with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were synthesized using three-level random-effects models, employing a restricted maximum likelihood estimator to account for between-study variance within a frequentist framework. Given that some studies reported distinct effect estimates corresponding to different DAT thresholds beyond 1 year (e.g. 1–3 years and >3 years), three-level meta-analytical models were implemented to accommodate this inherent dependency, assuming that effect sizes were hierarchically structured within individual studies. A two-tailed P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for pooled effect estimates. Heterogeneity across studies was quantified using the I 2 statistic, which estimates the proportion of total variability attributable to between-study differences. The Cochran's Q test was employed to formally assess heterogeneity. I 2 values were interpreted as follows: 0–30%, potentially negligible heterogeneity; 30–50%, moderate heterogeneity; 50–75%, substantial heterogeneity; and 75–100%, considerable heterogeneity. 29 To assess small-study effects and potential publication bias, contour-enhanced funnel plots depicting effect sizes against standard errors were generated. Subgroup analyses were performed to assess AF recurrence according to ablation modality (radiofrequency vs. cryoballoon), arrhythmia subtype (paroxysmal vs. persistent), study design (prospective vs. retrospective), and ablation strategy—specifically, whether adjunctive lesion sets beyond pulmonary vein isolation were employed [PVI (+)] or not (PVI only). To ensure consistency with contemporary procedural standards, ablation strategies were classified in accordance with the 2024 European Heart Rhythm Association/Heart Rhythm Society/Asia Pacific Heart Rhythm Society/Latin American Heart Rhythm Society (EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS) expert consensus statement on catheter and surgical ablation of AF. 7 In this framework, adjunctive ablation was defined as the addition of one or more of the following lesion sets to PVI: cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation, linear lesions (e.g. roof or mitral isthmus lines), complex fractionated atrial electrogram ablation, posterior wall isolation, substrate modification targeting low-voltage areas, vein of Marshall ablation, non-pulmonary vein trigger ablation, or ganglionated plexi ablation. This classification reflects current expert consensus and was used to ensure methodological rigour and clinical relevance in our stratified analyses. 12 Additionally, age-stratified analyses were performed for both the primary outcome and AF subtype, evaluating the differential impact of early vs. delayed ablation across age groups. Based on the age distribution of study participants, four age strata were defined: (i) <55 years, (ii) 55–59 years, (iii) 60–64 years, and (iv) ≥65 years. Sensitivity analysis To ensure the robustness of the pooled estimates for the primary outcome, we conducted a series of leave-one-out meta-analyses, systematically omitting one study at a time to evaluate its influence on the overall effect size estimate and identify any disproportionately influential studies. Furthermore, given that the conversion of binomial data to HRs led to the incorporation of unadjusted estimates into the pooled analysis, we conducted a sensitivity analysis restricted to studies reporting adjusted HRs that accounted for potential baseline confounders. This supplementary analysis aimed to evaluate the potential influence of disparities in baseline patient characteristics and strengthen the validity of the effect estimates by minimizing residual confounding. Meta-regression analysis To investigate potential sources of heterogeneity and effect modifiers across the included studies, univariate meta-regression analyses were performed using a frequentist framework, contingent upon the availability of a sufficient number of studies. 21 The meta-regression models incorporated the following covariates: difference in mean DAT between early and delayed ablation groups, follow-up duration, proportion of male participants, BMI, prevalence of baseline comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension, OSA, history of heart failure, stroke, or coronary artery disease), baseline LAD, LVEF, use of AADs or beta-blockers, CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, and year of studies’ publication. These analyses aimed to identify variables influencing the observed effect estimates and to further elucidate potential determinants of variability in the meta-analytic findings. Results Study selection and characteristics The PRISMA flow diagram, outlining the systematic database search and study selection process, is presented in Supplementary material online , Figure S1 . Following the removal of duplicates, a total of 3891 records were initially retrieved and subjected to title and abstract screening. Of these, 3838 records were excluded based on relevance. The remaining 53 studies underwent a rigorous full-text evaluation, ultimately yielding 28 studies that met the predefined eligibility criteria. 30–57 A detailed account of excluded studies, along with the corresponding reasons for exclusion, is provided in Supplementary material online , Table S4 . The key characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table 1 and Supplementary material online , Table S5 , while Supplementary material online , Table S6 provides the list of variables used for confounder adjustment in the primary studies. Details of ablation strategies are provided in Supplementary material online , Table S7 , while the follow-up monitoring methods used to ascertain AF recurrence are presented in Supplementary material online , Table S8 . The definition of serious adverse events reported across included studies is detailed in Supplementary material online , Table S9 . A total of 28 studies, encompassing 41 431 patients who underwent their first AF ablation, were analysed. The study population comprised 65% male participants, with mean ages ranging from 39 to 70 years. The median follow-up duration was 24 months (interquartile range: 12–36 months). Regarding the timing of ablation, the earliest recorded DAT in the early and delayed ablation groups was 2.4 months and 14 months, respectively, whereas the longest DAT extended to 9.6 months and 136 months, respectively. At the time of diagnosis, PAF and PsAF were reported in 53% and 45% of patients, respectively. The ROBINS-I assessment indicated that most studies had a low risk of bias. Two studies 37 , 44 were rated as having serious concerns due to potential biases in outcome measurement and intervention classification (see Supplementary material online , Table 10 ). Atrial fibrillation recurrence A total of 26 studies, encompassing 39 903 patients with AF, evaluated the impact of DAT on AF recurrence, using a 1-year threshold to define early ablation. Over a median follow-up of 24 months, patients who underwent ablation within ≤1 year of diagnosis exhibited a significantly lower risk of AF recurrence compared to those with a DAT > 1 year [HR = 0.65, 95% CI = (0.59, 0.73), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 59%, heterogeneity P < 0.01; Figure 1 ]. These findings remained consistent in a sensitivity analysis restricted to studies reporting adjusted HRs, demonstrating a comparable risk reduction [aHR = 0.65, 95% CI = (0.57, 0.74), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 62%, heterogeneity P < 0.01; Supplementary material online , Figure S2 ]. Figure 1 Forest plots depicting the impact of DAT on AF recurrence, comparing individuals with a DAT of ≤1 year vs. >1 year. AF, atrial fibrillation; CI, confidence interval; DAT, diagnosis-to-ablation time; HR, hazard ratio. Based on a subgroup analysis, the benefit of early ablation within the first year of AF diagnosis was consistent for both PAF [ n = 13,063, HR = 0.72, 95% CI = (0.67, 0.77), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 36%, heterogeneity P = 0.11] and PsAF [ n = 10,771, HR = 0.70, 95% CI = (0.61, 0.81), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 59%, heterogeneity P < 0.01; Figure 2 ]. Subgroup analysis comparing studies employing PVI alone vs. those utilizing adjunctive lesion sets demonstrated no significant differences ( P = 0.38), with the association between early ablation and reduced AF recurrence remaining consistent across both subgroups ( Figure 3 ). Furthermore, individuals who underwent radiofrequency ablation within ≤1 year of diagnosis experienced a greater reduction in AF recurrence risk compared to those who underwent cryoballoon ablation [aHR = 0.43, 95% CI = (0.43, 0.67), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 59%, heterogeneity P < 0.01, vs. aHR = 0.74, 95% CI = (0.66, 0.82), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 16%, heterogeneity P = 0.31; Supplementary material online , Figure S3 ]. This favourable association with early ablation was consistent across both prospective and retrospective studies, although significant heterogeneity persisted in the pooled analysis of prospective studies (see Supplementary material online , Figure S4 ). The age-stratified analysis revealed that the benefit of early ablation was consistently observed across all age groups, with the greatest advantage observed in individuals younger than 55 years [HR = 0.49, 95% CI = (0.34, 0.71), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 72%, heterogeneity P = 0.01; Figure 3 ]. However, the magnitude of the benefit was inversely associated with increasing age [≥55 and <60 years, HR = 0.53, 95% CI = (0.35, 0.79), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 52%, heterogeneity P = 0.03; ≥60 and <65 years, HR = 0.66, 95% CI = (0.54, 0.81), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 73%, heterogeneity P < 0.01; ≥65 years, HR = 0.65, 95% CI = (0.59, 0.71), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 0%, heterogeneity P = 0.91; Figure 4 ). A similar age-dependent trend was observed within the PAF and PsAF subgroups (see Supplementary material online , Figure S5 ). Individuals with a DAT of ≤3 years exhibited a significantly lower risk of AF recurrence compared to those with a DAT > 3 years [eight studies ( n = 17 655), HR = 0.70, 95% CI = (0.67, 0.74), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 54%, heterogeneity P = 0.03; Supplementary material online , Figure S6 ). Moreover, the risk of AF recurrence increased by 10% for each additional year elapsed from AF diagnosis [HR = 1.10, 95% CI = (1.06, 1.15), P < 0.001; I 2 = 82%, heterogeneity P < 0.01; Supplementary material online , Figure S7 ]. The contour-enhanced funnel plot, depicting the relationship between effect size and standard error for the assessment of small-study effects and publication bias, is presented in Supplementary material online , Figure S8 . The sensitivity analysis, utilizing a leave-one-out approach, revealed no outliers or influential studies that significantly impacted the pooled effect estimates (see Supplementary material online , Figure S9 ). Meta-regression analysis The results of the meta-regression analyses are presented in Figure 5 . These analyses showed that a larger gap in DAT between early and delayed ablation groups was significantly associated with a lower risk of AF recurrence in the early ablation group. Additionally, a higher CHA₂DS₂-VASc score correlated with a reduced risk of AF recurrence among patients undergoing early AF ablation, compared to delayed ablation. Studies with an increased prevalence of heart failure among participants reported a significantly lower risk of AF recurrence in the early ablation group compared to the delayed ablation group. Baseline left LVEF emerged as a significant moderator of the pooled risk, with the benefit from early ablation procedure being more pronounced in patients with lower LVEF. No significant effect modification was observed for the other covariates (see Supplementary material online , Figures S10 – S13 ). Moreover, most of the meta-regression analyses did not explain a substantial proportion of heterogeneity, as indicated by the R 2 values. DAT, diagnosis-to-ablation time; HF, heart failure; LVEF, left ventricular ejection fraction. Repeat ablation and new cardioversion The risk of repeat ablation was significantly lower in individuals with a DAT duration of ≤1 year compared to those with a DAT duration of >1 year [nine studies ( n = 6865), risk ratio (RR) = 0.70, 95% CI = (0.51, 0.95), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 59%, heterogeneity P = 0.01; Figure 6A ]. Similarly, the risk of new cardioversion was significantly lower in the ≤1-year DAT group than in the >1-year DAT group [six studies ( n = 5761), RR = 0.60, 95% CI = (0.48, 0.74), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 0%, heterogeneity P = 0.47; Figure 6B ). Figure 6 Forest plots illustrating the impact of DAT on repeat ablation ( A ), new cardioversion ( B ), cardiovascular hospitalization ( C ), cardiovascular mortality ( D ), and all-cause mortality ( E ) in individuals with a DAT of ≤1 year vs. >1 year. CI, confidence interval; DAT, diagnosis-to-ablation time; RR, risk ratio. Cardiovascular hospitalization and mortality Diagnosis-to-ablation time of ≤1 year was significantly associated with a reduced risk of cardiovascular hospitalization [eight studies ( n = 8373), RR = 0.74, 95% CI = (0.63, 0.88), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 44%, heterogeneity P = 0.08; Figure 6C ). However, no significant differences were observed in the risk of cardiovascular or all-cause mortality when using a DAT threshold of 1 year ( Figures 6D and E ). Serious periprocedural adverse events The risk of serious periprocedural adverse events did not differ significantly between patients with DAT duration of ≤1 year and >1 year [RR = 0.76, 95% CI = (0.54, 1.05), P < 0.0001; I 2 = 6%, heterogeneity P = 0.38; Supplementary material online, Figure 14 ]. Use of antiarrhythmic medication prior to index ablation Patients with a DAT duration of ≤1 year had significantly lower odds of receiving AADs prior to the ablation procedure compared to those with a longer DAT [odds ratio OR = 0.75, 95% CI = (0.60, 0.93), P < 0.001; I 2 = 75%, heterogeneity P < 0.01; Figure 7 ].
