UA, uric acid; WBC, white blood cell Quality assessment The detailed AHRQ and NOS scores for each study are presented in Tables S1 and S2 . For cross-sectional studies, six studies received an AHRQ score of 8, indicating high quality [ 22 , 24 – 26 , 29 , 30 ]. Quality scores were mainly penalized for unclear or missing information on blinding of subjective-component evaluators, handling of missing data, and follow-up. The methodological quality of the included cohort study was evaluated using the NOS, which assesses three domains: selection, comparability, and outcome assessment or follow-up. For studies on SHR and CAD severity, quality scores were penalized for hospital-based control selection, pre-existing disease history, or lack of blinding. For studies on prognosis, quality scores were mainly penalized for inadequate follow-up time or non-blinded assessment. All studies achieved a high NOS score (typically the final score ≥ 6), indicating good quality. Scores of 7, 8, and 9 were assigned to 5 studies [ 23 , 27 , 28 , 31 , 51 ], 18 studies [ 32 , 34 – 36 , 38 – 41 , 45 – 50 , 52 , 54 , 59 , 60 ], and 11 studies [ 9 , 33 , 37 , 42 – 44 , 53 , 55 – 58 ], respectively. SHR and CAD severity Existing evidence on the relationship between SHR and CAD severity remains limited, with only 9 studies [ 22 – 30 ] addressing this association. Given the diversity of outcome endpoints across these studies, which precluded data pooling, we conducted a descriptive analysis. In brief, among patients with CAD, SHR is associated with a higher incidence of multi-vessel lesion (categorical: OR = 1.86, 95% CI 1.272–2.719, P = 0.001; continuous: OR = 4.047, 95% CI 2.137–7.663, P < 0.001) [ 22 ] and in-stent restenosis (continuous: OR = 32.05, 95% CI 6.827–150.450, P < 0.05) [ 23 ]. In patients with ACS, a categorical analysis of SHR revealed that higher levels were associated with an increased risk of large thrombus burden [ 24 ], microvascular obstruction [ 26 ], and mid-to-high SYNTAX scores [ 27 ]. When SHR was analyzed as a continuous variable, elevated levels were associated with higher risks of large thrombus burden [ 25 ], NTL progression [ 28 ], no-reflow phenomenon [ 29 ], and in-hospital stent thrombosis [ 30 ]. Table 1 summarizes the key details of these studies. SHR and CAD prognosis A total of 36 studies [ 9 , 31 – 65 ] investigated the relationship between SHR and CAD prognosis. Seven of these studies used data from the MIMIC-IV or CIN-II databases [ 41 , 45 , 60 , 62 – 65 ]. Cui [ 37 ] and Fu [ 61 ] analyzed the same population from the China Acute Myocardial Infarction Registry. After study selection, twenty-two studies [ 9 , 31 – 51 ] were included for ACS, nine for chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) [ 34 , 43 , 54 – 60 ], and two for myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) [ 52 , 53 ]. Table 2 summarizes the characteristics of the included studies, and Table S3 details the MACE definitions adopted by each study. Prognosis of ACS and MINOCA When the outcomes were reported as HR, pooling data from 8 studies [ 33 , 35 , 42 , 43 , 46 – 48 , 50 ] demonstrated that patients with ACS with the highest SHR levels had a significantly increased risk of MACE compared to those with the lowest levels (HR: 1.60, 95% CI 1.41–1.81, I 2 = 56%, P < 0.00001). A similar prognostic association was observed in a subgroup analysis of five studies [ 9 , 42 , 43 , 46 , 50 ] assessing SHR as a continuous variable, yielding an HR of 1.59 (95% CI 1.27–2.00, I 2 = 77%, P < 0.0001 per unit increment). When the outcomes were reported as OR, pooling data from two studies [ 40 , 49 ] revealed a significant association between elevated SHR levels and MACE risk (OR: 1.58, 95% CI 1.19–2.11, I 2 = 0%, P = 0.002 for highest vs. lowest categories). Furthermore, a continuous variable analysis of three studies [ 38 , 40 , 46 ] confirmed this risk (OR: 3.50, 95% CI 1.47–8.32, I 2 = 87%, P = 0.006 per unit increment) (Figs. 2 and S1 , Table S4 ). Fig. 2 The pooled result of the incidence rate of the clinical endpoint in ACS patients For secondary endpoints, the pooled analysis of 9 studies [ 31 , 33 , 35 , 37 , 41 – 43 , 50 , 51 ] treating SHR as a categorical variable showed a significant association between the highest SHR level and all-cause death (HR: 1.54, 95% CI 1.40–1.68, I 2 = 0%, P < 0.00001). In addition, seven studies [ 9 , 37 , 39 , 41 – 43 , 50 ] analyzing SHR as a continuous variable reported an HR of 1.48 (95% CI 1.26–1.74, I 2 = 86%, P < 0.00001 per unit increment). When the outcomes were reported as OR, pooling data from six studies [ 32 , 34 , 36 , 37 , 45 , 51 ] demonstrated that high SHR implies a greater likelihood of all-cause death (OR: 2.59, 95% CI 2.02–3.33, I 2 = 67%, P < 0.001). This prognostic impact remained consistent in a continuous variable subset analysis involving four studies [ 34 , 37 , 45 ] (OR: 2.77, 95% CI 1.53–5.04, I 2 = 96%, P = 0.0008 per unit increment). More detailed results for the secondary outcomes are presented in Figs. 2 and S1 . In patients with MINOCA, Abdu [ 52 ] and Gao [ 53 ] analyzed SHR as a categorical variable and found that those with the highest SHR levels had a 2.57-fold increased risk of MACE (95% CI 1.86–3.55, I 2 = 0%, P < 0.00001). Gao [ 53 ] also reported a significant association between each SD increase in SHR and MACE (HR: 2.30, 95% CI 1.21–4.38, P = 0.01). Prognosis for CCS Pooling data from six studies [ 43 , 54 – 57 , 59 ] demonstrated that high SHR implies a significantly higher risk of MACE (HR: 1.95, 95% CI 1.50–2.52, I 2 = 77%, P < 0.00001). This prognostic impact remained consistent in a continuous variable subset analysis involving three studies [ 43 , 56 , 59 ] (HR: 1.87, 95% CI 1.64–2.12, I 2 = 0%, P < 0.00001 per unit increment) (Fig. 3 ). More detailed results are presented in Figure S2 and Table S4 . Fig. 3 The pooled result of the incidence rate of the clinical endpoint in CCS patients For secondary endpoints, when the outcomes were reported as HR, the pooled analysis of three studies [ 43 , 54 , 58 ] showed that patients with CCS with the highest SHR levels had a significantly higher risk of all-cause mortality than those in the lowest category (HR: 1.63, 95% CI 1.24–2.13, I 2 = 32%, P = 0.0004). In contrast, Lin [ 43 ] reported that as a continuous variable, no statistically significant association was observed between each unit increase in SHR and all-cause mortality (HR: 1.44, 95% CI 0.33–6.32, P = 0.63). Data on all-cause mortality were limited to a single study, which reported significantly elevated ORs for both categorical SHR (OR: 3.56, 95% CI 1.57–8.11, P = 0.002) and continuous SHR (OR: 15.45, 95% CI 6.92–34.49, P < 0.00001 per unit increment). The detailed results for secondary outcomes are shown in Figs. 3 and S2 . Subgroup analysis of SHR and endpoints Owing to the variability in definitions and cutoff values across studies, subgroup stratifications were performed based on the categories reported in the original studies. These analyses were stratified by: age (young vs. old) [ 46 , 48 , 50 ], sex (female vs. male) [ 46 , 48 , 50 ], body mass index (low vs. high) [ 46 , 48 , 50 ], diabetes status (yes vs. no) [ 33 , 35 , 42 , 46 – 48 , 50 ], smoking status (yes vs. no) [ 46 , 50 ], hypertension (yes vs. no) [ 46 , 50 ], initial diagnosis (NSTEMI vs. STEMI) [ 46 , 48 ], and left ventricular ejection fraction (low vs. high) [ 48 , 50 ]. The specific criteria for subgroup definitions vary and are listed in Table S5 . In ACS, no significant interaction between SHR and any stratification factor was observed for MACE, confirming a consistent association across subgroups (all P for interactio n > 0.05) (Fig. 4 ). Owing to the limited number of studies, we performed a subgroup analysis for patients with CCS focusing on diabetes status. The relationship between SHR and MACE remained consistent (Fig. 4 ). Further subgroup analyses stratified by mortality type (long-term vs. in-hospital) in the ACS cohort confirmed that SHR was significantly associated with both endpoints, regardless of whether HR or OR were reported (Fig. S3 ). Fig. 4 Subgroup analysis for SHR and MACE in ACS and CCS patients Publication bias and GRADE certainty Figure S4 illustrates the funnel plots for the associations between SHR and MACE or all-cause mortality in the ACS and CCS cohorts. Egger’s tests indicated significant publication bias within the ACS cohort for specific categorical (HR-MACE, P = 0.0317; OR-all-cause mortality, P = 0.0393) and continuous SHR analyses (HR-all-cause mortality, P = 0.0029; OR-MACE, P = 0.0127; OR-all-cause mortality, P = 0.0015). No significant bias was observed in the remaining comparisons ( P > 0.05). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses are displayed in Fig. S5 . While significant heterogeneity remained in most of the studies, the direction of the effect estimates was generally preserved across all scenarios. These results support the stability of the primary association, indicating that any single study does not heavily influence it. As the analyses were restricted to non-randomized studies, the baseline certainty of evidence was low. Subsequent downgrades for inconsistency and publication bias resulted in low or very low certainty for all outcomes (Tables S6 – S9 ). Discussion Main finding SHR provides a quick and cost-effective measure for acute hyperglycemia, reflecting an individual’s physiological response to stress. The main findings of this meta-analysis demonstrate that higher SHR levels are associated with more severe CAD. Elevated SHR consistently predicts a greater risk of adverse outcomes in patients with ACS and CCS (Fig. 5 ). Fig. 5 The summary of the study Higher SHR is associated with higher CAD severity Chronic hyperglycemia is a well-established factor influencing CAD severity. HbA1c shows a linear relationship with CAD burden, even in individuals without diabetes, and remains an independent predictor of more extensive disease and higher SYNTAX scores [ 66 ]. Increasing evidence indicates that fluctuations in glucose levels may cause greater vascular damage than sustained hyperglycemia by amplifying endothelial dysfunction and oxidative stress [ 67 , 68 ]. Acute glycemic swings promote matrix metalloproteinase activity, accelerate fibrous-cap degradation, destabilize coronary plaques, and enhance LDL oxidation, foam-cell formation, and vascular smooth muscle cell apoptosis and necrosis [ 69 ]. Furthermore, SH is driven by neuroendocrine dysregulation and systemic inflammation, which trigger the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1 (IL-1), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) [ 70 , 71 ]. These cytokines contribute to atherogenesis through multiple intracellular signaling pathways [ 72 , 73 ]. Zhang et al. [ 22 ] reported that individuals with multi-vessel CAD were older, exhibited higher SHR values, and showed a greater prevalence of glucose-metabolism disturbances than those with single-vessel disease. Zhao et al. [ 27 ] identified a U-shaped association between SHR and CAD complexity in patients with ACS, with an SHR interval of 0.68–0.875 corresponding to the lowest risk of intermediate-to-high SYNTAX scores. Liu et al. [ 28 ] also demonstrated that higher SHR levels were closely associated with the progression of non-target lesions. Acute hyperglycemia is closely associated with prothrombotic diathesis through the strong activation of the coagulation cascade [ 74 ]. Circulating levels of several procoagulant factors increase, whereas fibrinolytic activity decreases in patients with diabetes mellitus [ 75 ]. Hyperglycemia increases plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 levels, reduces fibrinolysis, and promotes thrombus formation [ 76 ], contributing to intracoronary thrombogenesis. In a study by Chu et al. [ 74 ], higher SHR values were strongly correlated with larger thrombus burden, which may partially explain the increased incidence rates of in-stent restenosis [ 30 ] and the no-reflow phenomenon observed after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) [ 29 ]. Mone et al. reported that SHR is an independent risk factor for hospitalization in patients with INOCA due to chest pain, likely reflecting hyperglycemia-induced microvascular dysfunction [ 77 ], with or without diabetes. Higher SHR is associated with poorer CAD prognosis Elevated SHR predicts adverse outcomes across the entire CAD spectrum, including ACS and CCS. In patients with ACS, hyperglycemia stimulates cardiac inducible nitric oxide (NO) synthase, increasing NO production, which reacts with superoxide to form peroxynitrite, a potent oxidant that damages cardiomyocytes and promotes tyrosine nitration [ 78 ]. Hyperglycemia also triggers the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6, which enhance mitochondrial reactive oxygen species generation and elevate C-reactive protein levels [ 52 , 79 ]. These inflammatory and vasoconstrictive responses impair coronary endothelial function and contribute to myocardial ischaemia. The cumulative cardiotoxic effects of SH may account for the increased incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with ACS with obstructive disease, and in those with MINOCA [ 80 ]. Importantly, subgroup analyses demonstrated that this association remained consistent across clinical subgroups, with no significant interaction effects, supporting the robustness and broad applicability of this finding. In predicting 1-year all-cause mortality among diabetic patients with STEMI, SHR outperformed other glucose-related measures, including optimal blood glucose, HbA1c, and the glucose/HbA1c ratio (GHR) [ 32 ]. In addition, incorporating SHR into risk models significantly enhances the prediction of in-hospital mortality in patients with AMI beyond traditional risk factors [ 37 ]. These findings highlight the prognostic importance of the magnitude of glucose elevation relative to the baseline at presentation [ 81 ]. Cardiac MRI studies further demonstrated that SHR is inversely associated with left ventricular ejection fraction and independently predicts microvascular obstruction [ 26 ]. Elevated SHR also predicts a higher risk of post-PCI complications in patients with ACS [ 40 ], including pulmonary infection, major bleeding [ 51 ], and mechanical adverse events [ 82 ]. Even in the absence of acute stress, SHR reflects underlying glucose metabolic dysregulation driven by cumulative chronic low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress [ 83 ]. Consequently, SHR maintains independent prognostic significance in patients with CCS undergoing PCI or CABG [ 54 , 59 ]. Xu et al. [ 34 ] reported that higher SHR predicted in-hospital mortality even without overt stress, highlighting its relevance beyond acute scenarios. However, because SH is primarily a transient neuro-endocrine response, its ability to predict long-term mortality in stable coronary disease remains uncertain [ 84 ]. Song et al. [ 55 ] found that in patients with chronic total occlusions followed for three years, higher SHR was associated with increased cardiac death and target-vessel myocardial infarction, particularly among individuals with pre-diabetes or type 2 diabetes. This effect appeared to be mediated by inflammation, as SHR was closely correlated with high-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels. In patients with CAD after CABG, elevated SHR is significantly associated with perioperative complications, including postoperative delirium [ 85 ] and atrial fibrillation [ 86 ]. Lei et al. [ 87 ] emphasized that the incremental prognostic value of SHR supports its utility for risk stratification, particularly for short-term outcomes. However, its predictive value for long-term mortality declines over time, indicating that other factors, such as chronic comorbidities and post-discharge care, might play a more dominant role in late-stage mortality. Future studies should identify the specific patient subgroups that would derive the greatest clinical benefit from SHR-guided risk stratification. Current stage and future prospects SHR is calculated by dividing ABG or FBG concentration by the estimated average glucose level, allowing a more precise assessment of stress-induced hyperglycemia than ABG or FBG alone. However, there is no consensus on the optimal method for estimating the average glucose value. Glycated albumin, which is unaffected by renal insufficiency or anaemia, may provide a more accurate estimate [ 88 , 89 ]. In a study of 1,643 patients with STEMI undergoing primary PCI, Liao et al. [ 39 ] compared SHR calculated from HbA1c and glycated albumin and found that both formulas had similar discriminative ability for predicting in-hospital mortality. Both indices outperformed the traditional risk models, with the glycated albumin-based SHR showing a slightly higher C statistic [ 39 ]. Insulin resistance and chronic inflammation are integral to the progression of coronary artery disease; thus, combining SHR with other cardiometabolic markers may provide a more comprehensive assessment of an individual’s metabolic risk. For instance, both the TyG index [ 90 , 91 ] and SHR [ 92 ] reflect the concurrent inflammatory activation, and simultaneous elevations of the TyG index and SHR indicate the presence of chronic and acute metabolic stress, which amplifies inflammatory signaling pathways. In patients with ACS and CCS, combining the TyG index and SHR offers additional prognostic insight for adverse clinical outcomes [ 55 , 93 – 96 ]. Moreover, combining other parameters, such as estimated glucose disposal rate and systemic inflammation response index, might also provide new complementary insights from a multidimensional perspective [ 97 – 99 ]. Current strategies for managing SH include insulin monotherapy or glucose-insulin-potassium (GIK) infusion. Evidence indicates that GIK may be associated with higher mortality compared with controls, whereas insulin effectively reduces acute hyperglycemic complications, making it the preferred option in critical care settings [ 100 ]. However, the optimal glycemic targets remain contentious. Tight control (80–110 mg/dL) improves survival in non-diabetic ICU patients, but similar aggressive targets increase mortality in patients with diabetes [ 101 ]. To date, no studies have evaluated longitudinal changes in SHR or their effects on long-term outcomes. Future research should integrate SHR-based risk stratification into glucose management protocols to minimize glycemic fluctuations, and prospective trials are required to test tiered insulin–glucose strategies guided by SHR thresholds. Repeated SHR measurements may further enhance risk prediction, as patients whose SHR increases after an initially elevated baseline are likely to have worse outcomes than those whose ratio declines [ 102 ]. Strengths and limitations As the first registered systematic review and meta-analysis to compile all available evidence on SHR in CAD, this study provides a robust basis for clinical decision-making. Our findings indicate that SHR is a reliable indicator of CAD severity and a predictor of prognosis. However, several limitations require consideration. First, although pooled estimates were derived from multivariable-adjusted or propensity-score-matched analyses, the heterogeneity remained high, and residual confounding factors, such as the effects of antihyperglycemic medications during the acute phase and ICU energy intake, cannot be entirely excluded. In addition, blood glucose variability in prediabetic individuals differs from that in normoglycemic patients, and differences in the interval between symptom onset and ABG measurement at admission may have influenced the results. Most of the included studies were conducted in Asian populations, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other ethnic groups. Furthermore, a causal relationship between elevated SHR and increased CAD risk or severity cannot be firmly established due to the mixture of cross-sectional and longitudinal data. Finally, most studies measured SHR only at baseline, and data on longitudinal medication use, risk-factor management, and lifestyle changes during follow-up are limited. Conclusions SHR is an easily calculated, composite measure that mirrors the anatomical burden of CAD and provides incremental prognostic value beyond conventional cardiovascular risk factors. Future studies, such as mechanistic validation, glucose-targeted therapies, SHR-based risk stratification protocols, and repeated SHR monitoring, are required to determine whether SHR-guided interventions can improve outcomes of patients with CAD. documents.title: Risk of New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation in Opioid Users: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on 24,006,367 Participants.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite ongoing efforts, the prescription of opioids is still common. Long-term opioid use has been associated with an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: We aimed to evaluate the association between opioid use and the risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation.
METHODS: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies retrieved from MEDLINE and EMBASE databases according to PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines from inception to 29 January, 2024. The protocol was registered at PROSPERO (CRD42024512500). Two authors independently screened and extracted data from included studies. The quantitative analysis included only observational studies and results were synthesised by a pooled hazard ratio. Risk of bias was performed according to the ROBINS-I Cochrane tool, and the summary of evidence according to GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations).
RESULTS: Four out of 782 studies met the inclusion criteria for a quantitative analysis with 24,006,367 participants. Overall, 153,734 were opioid users. The proportion of women ranged from 13.2 to 100% and the median age ranged from 34 to 65 years. Studies reported 991,263 cases of new-onset atrial fibrillation. The pooled analysis showed a significant association between use of opioids and new-onset atrial fibrillation (hazard ratio 1.96, 95% confidence interval 1.43-2.69 with high heterogeneity). A sensitivity analysis by removing the study with the largest cohort showed similar results to the main analysis. In the summary of findings, the certainty of the evidence according to GRADE was moderate.
CONCLUSIONS: We found a significant association between opioid use and the risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation. When prescribing opioids, the risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation should be considered, especially in the presence of other risk factors for atrial fibrillation.
documents.conclusions: We found a significant association between opioid use and the risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation. When prescribing opioids, the risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation should be considered, especially in the presence of other risk factors for atrial fibrillation.

Key Points Opioid use is associated with a higher risk of developing new-onset atrial fibrillation. This association was consistent across observational studies involving over 24 million participants. Prescription of opioids in patients with risk factors for new-onset atrial fibrillation should be cautious. Introduction Opioids are pain-relieving drugs used in a variety of clinical settings, from post-surgical to chronic or neoplastic pain management [ 1 ]. Over the years, opioid prescriptions have steadily increased, with more than 191 million prescriptions dispensed to American patients in 2017 [ 2 , 3 ]. Opioids have also played a central role in palliative care, including for patients with cardiovascular disease [ 4 ]. However, their use carries a risk of serious complications, including overdose. Indeed, 67,367 people died of drug overdoses in the USA in 2018, and opioids were suspected as a contributing cause in about two thirds of cases [ 5 ]. For this reason, growing concerns have emerged about the over-prescription and over-use of opioids in the last decade, so that the term “The Opioid Pandemic” has been coined [ 6 ]. The mechanism of action of opioids is mediated by the binding to opioid receptors MOR (µ-opioid receptor), DOR (δ-opioid receptor) and KOR (κ-opioid receptor), which are physiologically activated by endogenous opioid peptides, such as β-endorphin [ 1 ]. Opioids exert systemic effects that extend beyond analgesia, influencing various physiological systems. In the neural system, they stimulate dopamine release and positive reinforcement circuits by acting on GABA-ergic neurons; in the respiratory system, they reduce the tidal volume; and in the gastrointestinal tract, they decrease hydrochloric acid secretion and reduce the propulsive motility, often resulting in constipation. Finally, they also exert effects on the cardiovascular system [ 1 ]. In this context, opioid use has been associated with an increased probability of adverse outcomes in acute heart failure [ 7 ]: indeed, an analysis of the ADHERE cohort performed on 147,362 hospitalisations showed an increased risk of mechanical ventilation (15.4% vs 2.8%, p < 0.001), intensive care admission (38.7% vs 14.4%, p < 0.001) and mortality (13.0% vs 2.4%, p < 0.001) in opioid users [ 7 ]. Prolongation of the QT interval and ventricular arrhythmias are relatively uncommon adverse effects of opioid use [ 8 , 9 ]. However, evidence from the REGARDS cohort, which followed 29,025 participants over a median of 6 years, suggests a significant association between opioid use and increased arterial stiffness and cardiovascular mortality in women (hazard ratio [HR] 1.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.12–1.84) [ 10 ]. More recently, a risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) in opioid users has been reported [ 11 , 12 ]. This association is relevant because atrial fibrillation (AF) is already the most common supraventricular arrhythmia, especially in older people [ 13 ]. New-onset AF is associated with increased clinical complications such as a higher risk of thromboembolic stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, cognitive decline, depression, impaired quality of life and hospitalisations [ 14 ]. In addition, AF is associated with a 1.5- to 3.5-fold increase in mortality compared with the general population [ 15 ]. Finally, AF is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism [ 16 ], which is also common in patients with cancer [ 17 ]. Moreover, once AF is detected, anticoagulant therapy needs to be considered based on the thromboembolic risk, thus exposing patients to a bleeding risk [ 15 ]. This is of concern in patients with cancer as some types of cancer are associated with an increased risk of major and intracranial bleeding [ 18 ]. Despite the relevance of the topic and the number of patients potentially affected, there is no solid evidence on this issue. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to summarise the available evidence on the association between opioids and NOAF. Methods Search Strategy and Study Selection Process We searched MEDLINE (PubMed) and EMBASE from inception up to 29 January, 2024 to retrieve eligible records. The search strategy included “opiate”, “opioid”, “morphine”, “atrial fibrillation”, “AF”, and “new onset atrial fibrillation” both as MeSH and free terms, combined with Boolean operators with no filters applied. The complete search strategy is outlined in Table 1 of the Electronic Supplementary Material (ESM). We included records written in English, reporting the results of randomised clinical trials, observational studies and cross-sectional studies on NOAF in the systematic review. We excluded review articles, commentaries, congress abstracts, single-arm studies and studies with no outcomes. Two study authors (DM and GG) independently screened the retrieved citations by title and abstract. Potentially eligible articles were read in full text for final inclusion decision and disagreements were solved by collegial discussion with a third author (DP). This systematic review is registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024512500) and followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) international guidelines [ 19 , 20 ]. Participants/population. Patients with any indication to opioid treatment. Interventions. Use of opioids for any indication, regardless of the specific opioid type, dosage, route of administration or duration of use. Comparator. No opioid use. This may include patients receiving placebo, no treatment or alternative analgesic medications. Assessed Outcomes. Documented NOAF in patients with no history of clinically detected AF. Data Extraction Two authors (DM and GG) independently extracted data from included studies into an Excel spreadsheet. We collected the following information: first author, year of publication, study inclusion criteria, study design, the number of patients included and the number of patients taking opioids, age, sex, study follow-up, concomitant comorbidities such as proportion of patients with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease, smoking habit, obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome, and cancer and included the systematic review outcome. Discrepancies were solved by collegial discussion with a third author (DP). Risk of Bias Assessment and Publication Bias Two authors (IMP and AP) independently assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane Robins-I tool for observational studies, which evaluates the following domains: bias due to confounding, bias due to selection of participants, bias in classification of interventions, bias due to deviations from intended interventions, bias due to missing data, bias in measurement of outcomes and bias in selection of the reported results [ 21 ]. Robins I figures were created with the robvis online tool [ 22 ]. Publication bias was assessed with the realisation of funnel plots. Statistical Analysis If at least two included studies had available data for the assessed primary endpoint, we performed a random-effects Mantel–Haenszel meta-analysis to estimate the pooled HR with 95% CI. A random-effects model was selected a priori to account for heterogeneity across studies; the choice of model was informed by the anticipated variability across populations and interventions. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic, with thresholds of < 25%, 25–75% and > 75% interpreted as low, moderate and high heterogeneity, respectively. Only observational studies were included in the quantitative analysis. A further sensitivity analysis was performed by removing the study performed by Lin et al. [ 23 ] because of the size of the study cohort and replicating the meta-analysis. All statistical tests were two-sided, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The Cochrane RevMan 5.4 and R software (R Development Core Team, 2021) version 4.1.2. were used for the analyses. Summary of Findings Summary of findings was produced using GRADEproGDT. The quality of the evidence was evaluated with the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) method independently by two authors (GG and DM) and discrepancies were resolved by collegial discussion with a third author (DP). Ethics Approval and Informed Consent Ethics approval was not required because of the study type (systematic review and meta-analysis). Patients were not involved in the design and the development of this study. Results Search Results and Study Characteristics We identified 782 references from the literature (481 from EMBASE and 301 from MEDLINE [PubMed]). Of these, 769 were excluded after screening of titles and abstracts. The remaining 13 studies were examined and five [ 11 , 12 , 23 – 25 ] met the inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis. Of them, four provided data to be included in the meta-analysis [ 12 , 23 – 25 ] (Fig. 1 ). The study by Qureshi et al. [ 11 ] was included in the qualitative synthesis as it met the predefined inclusion criteria; however, it was excluded from the meta-analysis because of its cross-sectional design, which precluded the assessment of temporality between opioid use and incident AF. All studies were observational, no randomised controlled trials were found. Fig. 1 PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) flowchart The overall population included in the meta-analysis consisted of 24,006,367 participants (Table 1 ), of which 153,734 were opioid users (0.64%). During the follow-up, 991,263 new-onset AF cases occurred. Table 1 Clinical characteristics of studies included in the systematic review and meta-analysis Author, year FU (months) Clinical setting Total cohort Opioid users Age (median) Women (%) HTN (%) Diabetes (%) OSAS (%) CHD (%) Obesity (%) VHD (%) Alcohol (%) Smoking (%) Included in the systematic review Qureshi [ 11 ], 2015 NA REGARDS study participants 24,632 1887 65.0 54.0 – – – 17.4 – – 37.3 54.4 Included in the meta-analysis Lee [ 25 ], 2016 – Female patients with breast cancer 73,917 18,671 52.3 100.0 1.2 20.7 – – – 0.1 – – Harding [ 24 ], 2020 372 Adults 45–84 years of age free of cardiovascular disease 6652 636 62.0 47.0 33.0 12.3 3.3 – 32.5 – 55.9 13.5 Lin [ 23 ], 2022 – Adults seeking care in ED or clinic 23,316,035 10,032 46.6 55.0 18.0 9.0 1.0 4.2 3.8 1.3 0.8 4.9 Chui [ 12 ], 2024 144 Young veterans 609,763 124,395 34.0 13.2 15.8 2.5 6.2 1.1 39.9 – 12.2 43.7 CHD coronary heart disease, ED emergency department, FU follow-up, HTN hypertension, NA not applicable, OSAS obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome, VHD valvular heart disease One study enrolled only patients with cancer. The proportion of women ranged from 13.2 to 100%, as one study [ 25 ] enrolled only female patients with breast cancer. Median age ranged from 34 to 65 years (Table 1 ). The most represented ethnicity was Caucasian (38.3–57.8%) [Table 2 of the ESM]. A low proportion of patients had cardiovascular risk factors: indeed, hypertension and diabetes ranged between 1.2–3.0 and 2.5–20.7%, respectively. Furthermore, additional risk factors for NOAF such as alcohol use and smoking ranged between 0.8–55.9 and 4.9–54.4%, respectively. Further clinical information according to each study is reported in Table 1 . One out of four studies included in the meta-analysis was prospective [ 24 ] (Table 2 of the ESM), and all studies identified NOAF by the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision evaluating NOAF in patients with no previous clinical history of AF (Table 2 of the ESM). Further data on follow-up, type of opioid used, ethnicity, study design, and new-onset AF diagnosis and definition are reported in Table 2 of the ESM. Risk of Bias Assessment The risk of bias of the four observational studies included in the meta-analysis is represented in Panels A and B of Fig. 1 of the ESM. Two studies [ 12 , 25 ] were considered as having a low risk of bias across all key domains. One study [ 24 ] was rated as having a moderate risk of bias because of concerns in confounding, selection of participants, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data and selection of the reported results domains. One study [ 23 ] was judged to have a moderate risk of bias because of issues in the selection of participants (Panel A of Fig. 1 of the ESM). Overall, 75% of studies were at a low risk of bias for domains 1, 3, 4, 5 and 7 of the ROBINS-I tool, all studies had a low risk of bias for domain 6 and 50% of a low risk of bias for the remaining domain of ROBINS-I (Panel B of Fig. 1 of the ESM). No serious risk of bias was observed in any of the included studies. Opioids and New-Onset AF New-onset AF was the primary endpoint of all studies included in the meta-analysis. Four observational studies were included in the analysis (Fig. 2 , Panel A). All studies showed coherent results with a direct association between opioid use and new-onset AF. The pooled analysis, as reported in the forest plot, showed a strong association between the use of opioids and new-onset AF (HR 1.96, 95% CI 1.43–2.69). However, the heterogeneity among the study included is high ( I 2 = 97%). In the sensitivity analysis, removing the study performed by Lin et al. [ 23 ] because of the large study cohort, no substantial difference was observed (HR 1.60, 95% CI 1.51–1.70, I 2 = 98%) as compared with the main analysis (Fig. 2 , Panel B). Funnel plots did not show relevant publication bias (Fig. 2 of the ESM). Fig. 2 Forest plot of use of opioids and new-onset atrial fibrillation. Panel A : overall analysis. Panel B : sensitivity analysis removing Lin et al. CI confidence interval, df degree of freedom, IV inverse variance, SE standard error Summary of Findings The certainty of the evidence according to GRADE was moderate and the meta-analysis suggested that opioid use results in an increased risk of new-onset AF. We downgraded the certainty of evidence according to the risk of bias and the heterogeneity of the studies included. A summary of findings with a quality of evidence assessment according to the GRADE method is provided in Table 2 . Table 2 Summary of findings Outcomes Anticipated absolute effects c (95% CI) Relative effect (95% CI) No. of participants (studies) Certainty of the evidence (GRADE) Comments Risk with [comparison] Risk with [intervention] New-onset atrial fibrillation 42 per 1.000 80 per 1.000 (59–108) HR 1.96(1.43–2.69) 24,006,367 (4 observational studies) ⨁⨁⨁◯ Moderate a,b Opioid use results in an increased risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation CI confidence interval, GRADE Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations, HR hazard ratio a A moderate risk of bias for Domain 2 of the study performed by Lee et al.[ 25 ] b High heterogeneity among studies included c The risk in the intervention group (and its 95% CI) is based on the assumed risk in the comparison group and the relative effect of the intervention (and its 95% CI) Discussion In this meta-analysis, we provide pooled data supporting the evidence for a significant association between the use of opioids and new-onset AF in a large sample of population. We found a nearly doubled risk of NOAF in opioid users compared with non-users. Although several diseases and clinical conditions may require opioid prescriptions, the most common indication is to treat pain, especially acute pain, usually in patients with cancer [ 26 ]. In our meta-analysis, one study included patients with breast cancer only [ 25 ]. In this study, the risk of new-onset AF was increased more than four-fold exceeding the risk observed in other studies. These patients have also other risk factors for NOAF, including the cancer type itself because of higher inflammatory and oxidative pathways, as well as cancer treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy, use of non- steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and radiotherapy [ 27 ]. Uncontrolled pain may promote autonomic system dysfunction favouring electrical atrial remodelling and new-onset AF [ 27 ], and chronic pain as well has been linked to cardiac arrhythmias with evidence of a temporal and dose relationship [ 28 ]. It should be underlined that the coexistence of AF and cancer could worsen the prognosis of these patients, as shown in a large cohort of 1,585,760 Dutch patients [ 29 ], in which either cancer diagnosed after incident AF (HR 7.77, 95% CI 7.45–8.11) or AF diagnosed after incident cancer (HR 2.55, 95% CI 2.47–2.63) was associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality [ 29 ]. Therefore, it may be crucial to reduce the risk of NOAF in patients with cancer undergoing surgery, especially chest interventions, or chemotherapy, in which the risk of NOAF is higher [ 27 ]. It is essential, however, to distinguish between perioperative AF and NOAF occurring outside of surgical contexts, as they differ in pathogenesis and clinical implications. Perioperative AF is typically transient, driven by acute physiological stressors of surgery, such as anaesthesia, fluid shifts and systemic inflammation, and often resolves without long-term sequelae [ 30 ]. In contrast, NOAF arising outside the perioperative period may reflect more persistent underlying cardiac or systemic abnormalities and may carry a different prognostic burden. Recognising this distinction is key to guiding both acute management and long-term follow-up strategies in this high-risk population. Biological Plausibility Opioids bind to MORs, DORs and KORs, which, despite their subtype diversity, collectively activate G-proteins and by dimerisation promote signal cascades. Research indicates their involvement in cardiovascular homeostasis, with endogenous opioid peptides found in the heart and influencing the heart rate, contractility and vascular health [ 31 ]. Nevertheless, contrasting roles have been observed among receptor subtypes. Particularly, DORs have been linked to myocardial protection during ischaemia and resistance against oxidative stress through increasing intracellular calcium levels and protein kinase C pathway activation. In contrast, KORs have showed anti-preconditioning effects in murine models and have demonstrated arrhythmogenic potential in isolated perfused rat hearts [ 32 – 35 ]. Therefore, altering the physiological balance between DOR and KOR activation by administering opioids might play a role in AF genesis. In particular, in fibrillating human atria tissue, a downregulation of opioid receptor and ligand expression, potentially indicating a loss of protective capacity in fibrillating atrial tissue, has been observed [ 34 ]. Beyond direct pharmacodynamic effects, opioids have been shown to block the rapid component of the delayed rectifier potassium channel, which is crucial for diastolic potential restoration during repolarisation. This inhibition may prolong action potential duration and the QT interval, potentially leading to heterogeneous electrical states and arrhythmias [ 36 , 37 ]. Clinical Implications Our study has potentially relevant clinical and healthcare implications. Prescription of opioids should take into account the concomitant presence of other risk factors for NOAF either by a clinical evaluation (history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, thyroid disorders, recent major surgery, some types of cancer) or by using clinical risk scores (i.e., C 2 HEST score [ 38 ]) to identify patients at a higher risk of developing NOAF. The use of opioids should be carefully considered in high-risk patients (i.e., those with a C 2 HEST score >2), and a closer follow-up should be planned to early detect NOAF. In these patients, the use of alternative analgesic medications, such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs, should be considered and offered to patients, in line with the CDC Guidelines for prescribing opioids [ 39 ]. However, it is important to note that some NSAIDs have also been associated with an increased risk of AF [ 40 , 41 ]. Therefore, pain management strategies should be carefully personalised, taking into account each patient’s cardiovascular risk profile and overall clinical context. In this context, the aim of a comprehensive evaluation prior to prescribing opioids should ultimately be to reduce the risk of NOAF. This may in turn lower the risk of hospitalisation, as the management of NOAF may often require admission to the emergency department for acute rate or rhythm control [ 14 ]. In addition, once AF is established, patients face a substantially higher risk of hospital admission for both cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular causes compared with those without AF [ 42 ], along with increased ischaemic and bleeding complications, resulting in high healthcare costs [ 43 ]. Furthermore, the therapeutic management of AF in this setting can also be challenging, as some commonly used rate-control agents have been linked to less favourable outcomes, highlighting the importance of a preventative approach, rather than a curative approach, wherever possible [ 44 ]. Another important concern is related to an opioid overdose. The association between opioid use and AF also extends to overdose scenarios. A study performed on 430,460 adult hospitalisations showed that AF was the most frequent (4.1%) arrhythmia associated with opioid overdose [ 45 ]. Notably, the rate of hospitalisations for opioid overdose-related AF has risen significantly in recent years, increasing from 30 to 50 cases per 1000 hospitalisations ( P trend < 0.001) [ 45 ]. Limitations Despite the analysis being conducted on a population of > 24 million individuals, the heterogeneity among studies was high, indicating that further research on more homogenous sub-populations might be useful. This heterogeneity may reflect the wide use of opioids and the numerous clinical indications of these drugs, especially in relieving pain in patients with cancer or neurological disorders. Unfortunately, we could not perform a subgroup analysis by indication because of a lack of data. Furthermore, we could not evaluate the effect of different types of opioids or dosing because of the lack of information in the studies included. In this context, we can only provide an estimate of the risk of the onset of AF in users versus non-users of opioids. This relative risk should be interpreted also considering that other analgesic drugs such as NSAIDs may be associated with an increased risk of NOAF [ 46 ]. This is a limitation that has been noted in studies examining the association within medications of the same class and arrhythmic events [ 47 ]. Finally, the available evidence is derived from observational studies which, despite exhibiting a low-to-moderate risk of bias, do not permit a causal inference. In particular, because of the inherent limitations of the study design and suboptimal reporting across included studies, we were not able to account for residual potential confounders, including patients’ comorbidities (e.g., pulmonary conditions, endocrine disorders or renal disfunction), concomitant medications and socioeconomic factors. Ad hoc preclinical studies are needed to provide a more robust rationale for the association between opioid use and the risk of NOAF. Conclusions Opioid use may be associated with a higher risk of NOAF, with a moderate certainty of evidence. Prescription of opioids in patients with risk factors for NOAF should be cautious and based on a comprehensive evaluation of the risk-benefit profile. documents.title: Cryoballoon versus radiofrequency ablation for persistent atrial fibrillation: an updated systematic review and meta‑analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Compared with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) is more harmful and difficult to treat, and the efficacy of different catheter ablation for both also varies greatly. So this study aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of cryoballoon (CB) and radiofrequency (RF) ablation in the treatment of persistent AF.
METHODS: We searched the PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane library databases for studies comparing the efficacy and safety between CB and RF ablation for persistent AF. All included studies met our inclusion criteria.
RESULTS: A total of 11 studies, 2551 patients were enrolled in this study, including 1256 patients in CB group and 1295 patients in RF group. Meta-analysis results showed that the freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmia (ATA) recurrence was similar between the CB and RF groups (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.18, I2 16%). The results of repeated ablation events in the two groups were similar (OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.12, I245%), while the operative time in the CB group was shorter than that in the RF group (mean reduction 45.27 min, 95% CI 61.34 to 29.20 min, I2 95%). There was no significant difference in fluoroscopy time between the two groups (mean difference 2.12 min, 95% CI 7.83 to 12.07 min, I2 99%). The incidence of total complications was similar between the two groups (OR 1.08, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.58, I2 0%), but phrenic nerve palsy (PNP) was more likely to occur in the CB group (OR 4.84, 95% CI 1.84 to 12.71, I2 0%). The incidence of pericardial tamponade was not statistically different between the two groups (OR 0.72, 95% CI 00.32 to 1.58, I2 0%).
CONCLUSIONS: CB can be used as an alternative therapy to RF for persistent AF, both of which have considerable efficacy and safety. CB can significantly reduce the operation time with the probability of high PNP.

Keywords Persistent atrial fibrillation Cryoballoon ablation Radiofrequency ablation Meta-analysis pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2025 Introduction Catheter ablation has emerged as a well-established therapeutic intervention for atrial fibrillation (AF), with widespread clinical adoption. It achieves arrhythmia control through three principal mechanisms: elimination of AF triggers, electrophysiological substrate modification, and modulation of the autonomic nervous system [ 1 ]. Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) serves as the cornerstone strategy in catheter ablation for both paroxysmal and persistent AF. In recent years, besides traditional radiofrequency (RF) ablation therapy, an updated technique-cryoballoon ablation (CB) is widely used in the treatment of AF, especially paroxysmal AF [ 2 ]. The 2024 ESC Guidelines [ 3 ], which provide a Class I recommendation for PVI in paroxysmal AF and Class IIa recommendation for endoscopic and hybrid ablation procedures in symptomatic persistent AF refractory to antiarrhythmic drug (AAD) therapy. However, until now there have been a few articles to compare the efficacy of CB and RF ablation on persistent AF. This meta-analysis aims to compare the safety and efficacy of CB and RF ablation for the treatment of persistent AF. Methods The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) statement was used for the conduct of this meta-analysis [ 4 ]. Data sources and inclusion criteria Three databases, PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane library databases, were searched during the study and conducted from the data of 2003 to March 2024. The medical terms used in the search were ((((((("Radiofrequency Ablation"[Mesh]) OR (Ablation, Radiofrequency[Title/Abstract])) OR (Radio-Frequency Ablation[Title/Abstract])) OR (Ablation, Radio-Frequency[Title/Abstract])) OR (Radio Frequency Ablation[Title/Abstract])) OR (Ablation, Radio Frequency[Title/Abstract])) AND (persistent atrial fibrillation)) AND ((cryoballoon ablation) OR (cryoablation)).The inclusion criteria for this study, established a priori, were as follows: (1) The patient had a medical history of persAF; (2) The population enrolled must be ablation-naïve; (3) Studies regarding the safety and efficacy of CB and RF for persistent AF; (4) Follow-up time was greater than one year. Additionally, Manual search was performed by screening the references cited in this manuscript (backward citation tracking). Outcomes In this study, clinical efficacy and safety were selected as outcome indicators. Clinical efficacy was the primary end and assessed by the recurrence of AF/atrial tachycardia (AT) after the blanking period (BP). According to the 2024 European Heart Rhythm Association (EHRA) consensus, the blanking period has been redefined as 8 weeks following catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation [ 5 ]. However, all 11 included studies published prior to 2024 employed a BP definition of 3 months post-procedure [ 6 ]. Secondary outcomes included total procedural duration, fluoroscopy duration, and safety outcomes (total complications, phrenic nerve palsy (PNP), pericardial effusion, or tamponade). Data collection and quality assessment The selected articles in this meta-analysis were read and screened independently by inclusion and exclusion criteria. The above process was extracted independently by two calibrated examiners, and any disagreements were resolved through open discussion. The following study characteristics were retrieved: the first author of included studies, time of publication, sample size, ablation method, gender, age, time of follow-up, adverse events, interventions and outcome indicators. For all included studies, observational studies and randomized controlled trials used Newcastle–Ottawa Scale and RevMan 5.4 software for quality evaluation, respectively. Statistical analysis The included studies were tested for heterogeneity to ensure the reliability of the meta-analysis. The I 2 was used to access the heterogeneity of the test results [ 7 ]. I 2 > 50% and P < 0.1 represents significant heterogeneity among studies, and random-effects model was used for combining. If I 2 < 50% and P > 0.1, the heterogeneity among the test results was considered small, and a fixed-effects model was used for combining. Sources of heterogeneity were sensitivity analyzed by case-by-case literature exclusion or subgroup analysis. The studied indicators were collected and collated, and the meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager5.4 software. The dichotomous variables were described by odds ratio (OR), and the continuous variables were described by mean difference (MD). Each effect size was estimated with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI), and P < 0.05 was set for statistical significance. Result Study selection By searching three databases, a total of 1262 studies were selected for the first time(PubMed: 1,067; Embase: 120; Cochrane: 75), 70 duplicate literatures were eliminated, and 152 reviews, meta-analysis, case reports, conference abstracts, and letters were eliminated through the classification function of the database. After reading the title and abstract, 22 studies were confirmed for full reading. Eleven studies were excluded due to unavailability of original data, duplicate publication, and being non-original research. Finally, 11 studies were included in meta-analysis, including 3 randomized controlled trial (RCT) and 8 observational studies. The process of literature screening results is shown in Fig. 1 [ 8 – 18 ]. Notably, the studies by Guler et al. [ 19 ] and Kosmidou et al. [ 20 ] were not included because no separate comparison of CB and RF was made. The study by Gallagher et al. [ 21 ] was not included because the ablation protocol used in this study was different from other studies, and the purpose of the study was irrelevant to us. Hoffman et al.’s [ 22 ] study was not accepted because it did not extract useful data. Fig. 1 PRISMA Flow Diagram Characteristics and quality of studies 11 relevant studies were included in this meta-analysis, including a total of 2551 patients, 1256 patients in CB group and 1295 patients in RF group. The basic characteristics of the included studies are shown in Table 1 . Baseline patient characteristics are shown in Table 2 . For CB, most studies used second-generation balloons as the ablation protocol. For RF, most studies used the contact force (CF)—sensing catheters. In particular, Boveda et al.'s study used first-generation balloons and non-CF catheters [ 9 ]. The average follow-up time ranged from 12 to 48 months. Most studies monitor recurrent use Holter ECG for 1 to 7 days, Mörtsell et al. [ 12 ] and Yokokawa et al. [ 11 ] use Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device (CIED) and Implantable Loop Recorder (ILR) to monitor the recurrence of ATA, and Baimbetov et al. [ 17 ] use the Reveal XT Implantable loop recorder (Medtronic, Minnesota) to monitor relapse. After the CB group was isolated in the pulmonary veins, most studies were allowed to tinker with different additional ablation techniques. At subsequent follow-up, most studies also performed repeated ablation in patients with recurrent ATA. The quality of all studies on observational was evaluated using Newcastle–Ottawa Quality Assessments, and the scores of all studies were 7–9 points, indicating a low risk of bias and a high quality of the selected studies. The RCTs were assessed by the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool,which had some unclear risk of bias. The details about the author’s judgments of the risk of bias assessment are outlined in (supplementary material: Table S1, Fig. S1, Fig. S2). 54 ± 12 53 ± 14 46 ± 5 46 ± 6 The results of meta-analysis Freedom from recurrent ATA Among the included studies, 10 studies reported the occurrence of freedom from ATA events in patients, and the incidence of freedom from ATA events in the CB group and the RF group was 62.3% and 61.9%, respectively. After heterogeneity test: P = 0.29, I 2 = 16%, it was considered that the heterogeneity among the studies was minimal. A fixed-effect model analysis demonstrated no statistically significant difference between the two groups in outcomes for patients without ATA, with an OR of 1.00 (95% CI [0.85,1.18], P = 1.00; Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Freedom from recurrent ATA with RF vs. CB ablation Repeat ablation Among the included studies, 6 studies reported repeated ablation events in patients, and the incidence of repeated ablation events in the CB group and the RF group were 18.4% and 21.0%, respectively. After heterogeneity test: P = 0.10, I 2 = 45%, it was considered that the heterogeneity among studies was low. The fixed-effect model was used, and the results were as follows: OR = 0.85, 95% CI [0.64,1.12], P = 0.24 (Fig. 3 ), indicating that there was no statistical difference in repeated ablation of patients between the two groups. Fig. 3 Repeat ablation with RF vs. CB ablation Total procedural time and fluoroscopy time Total procedural time and fluoroscopy time were reported in 8 studies. The total procedural time in the CB group was shorter than that in the RF group, with an average shortening of 45.27 min (95% CI 61.34 to -29.20) (Fig. 4 A), and there was a significant statistical difference between the two groups. There was non-significantly shorter fluoroscopy time with CB compared with RF (MD = 2.12, 95%CI [− 7.83, 12.07], P = 0.68) (Fig. 4 B). Fig. 4 A Total procedural time with RF vs. CB ablation; B : Fluoroscopy time with RF vs. CB ablation Complications In our study, nine studies reported the occurrence of total complications in patients, and there was no statistical difference in the occurrence of complications between the CB group and the RF group (CB 0.6% vs. RF 0.5%, OR = 1.08, 95%CI [0.74,1.58], P = 0.68) (Fig. 5 A). PNP and cardiac tamponade were reported as stand-alone complication. In our meta-analysis, nine studies provided detailed data on the incidence of PNP following CB and RF ablation. All studies consistently reported a higher incidence of PNP in the CB group compared to the RF group, which aligns with the conclusions drawn from our pooled analysis (CB 1.9% vs. RF 0.1%, OR = 4.84, 95% CI [1.84,12.71], P = 0.001) (Fig. 5 B). Cardiac tamponade was reported in seven studies, and the results were as follows: OR = 0.72, 95% CI [0.32,1.58], P = 0.41 (Fig. 5 C), indicating that there was no statistical difference in the occurrence of pericardial tamponade events between the CB group and the RF group. Fig. 5 A Total complications with RF vs. CB ablation; B : PNP with RF vs. CB ablation; C : Cardiac tamponade with RF vs. CB ablation Subgroup analysis In our study, subgroup analysis comparing freedom from ATA recurrence between RF ablation with PVI alone and RF ablation combined with extra-PVI lesions (Fig. 6 A) revealed no significant difference between the two groups ( P = 0.97). The subgroup analysis demonstrated statistically significant differences in procedural duration ( P = 0.04) and fluoroscopy time ( P = 0.03). Notably, in studies limited to PVI-only RF ablation, cryoballoon (CB) technology was associated with reductions of 58.48 min in procedural time and 4.87 min in fluoroscopy time (Fig. 6 B, C). Fig. 6 A Subgroup analysis for freedom from ATA by trial RF ablation strategy (PVI only or additional ablation permitted) B : Subgroup analysis for procedure time by trial RF ablation strategy (PVI only or additional ablation permitted) C : Subgroup analysis for fluoroscopy time by trial RF ablation strategy (PVI only or additional ablation permitted) Variations in post-ablation monitoring modalities (e.g., Holter monitoring, ILRs, or CIEDs) may introduce heterogeneity in primary outcome ascertainment and thereby influence study conclusions. To further investigate this, we performed a prespecified subgroup analysis stratifying studies by monitoring sensitivity into high-sensitivity and low-sensitivity cohorts. The analysis revealed no difference in freedom from recurrent ATA by subgroup (P = 0.31), which contradicts findings from benchmark trials (e.g., CIRCA-DOSE). Detailed data and the corresponding forest plots are presented in Supplementary Fig. S3. Sensitivity analysis In the statistical analysis of the above 6 indicators, significant heterogeneity was found in the total procedural time and fluoroscopy time. Sensitivity analysis was conducted for these two indicators respectively. In terms of total procedural time, after excluding the study of Bisignani et al. [ 14 ], which had a significant outlier, the duration of surgery in the CB group was still shorter than that in the RF group, which was the same as the previous results. Kobori et al.'s study was also regarded as a significant outlier in perspective time, and there was still no significant difference between the results of the two groups after removal and re-analysis. Discussion Atrial fibrillation is the most common persistent tachyarrhythmia, and PVI has long been shown to be the cornerstone of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation [ 23 ]. In recent years, CB has become an alternative to conventional RF catheter ablation technology. Technically, compared to RF, CB has the advantages of simplified surgical procedures and a shorter learning curve [ 24 ]. In the study of STOP Persistent AF, 54.8% of patients who used CB for catheter ablation maintained sinus rhythm, so CB also had a higher success rate compared with RF [ 25 ]. Over the past 15 years, several studies have evaluated the efficacy of CB and RF in the treatment of persistent atrial fibrillation, and both have shown comparable efficacy. Therefore, CB’s application in persistent AF has been widely adopted. For patients undergoing PVI surgery, arrhythmia recurrence constitutes the most frequent cause of rehospitalization, accounting for 40–60% of readmissions within 1 year according to large-scale registries [ 26 , 27 ], so effectively reducing postoperative recurrence and complications is crucial to accelerate the rehabilitation process. However, although the efficacy of the two techniques is comparable, some people still relapse after PVI surgery, so we need to know the effectiveness and safety of both in patients with persistent atrial fibrillation. Main findings In the form of meta-analysis, the following conclusions were drawn by comparing the efficacy of CB and RF in the treatment of persistent atrial fibrillation: (1) Primary outcome: Freedom from recurrent ATA rates were similar between the two groups; (2) Secondary outcomes: There were no significant differences in repeat ablation, fluoroscopy time, total complications, and pericardial tamponade. Total procedural time of CB group was significantly shorter than that of RF group. PNP events occurred less in RF group. Our conclusions are consistent with the results of two previous meta-analyses by Liu et al. [ 28 ]and Kim et al. [ 29 ]. Efficacy There was no difference in ATA-free survival rate between the two groups of patients. This result has been confirmed by a large number of data. ATA recurrence during the post-ablation blanking BP is termed early recurrence and is not considered indicative of procedural failure, as these episodes generally resolve spontaneously and typically do not warrant repeat ablation [ 5 ]. Conversely, recurrence after the 12-month postoperative period is classified as late recurrence, primarily attributed to progressive atrial fibrosis, sustained inflammatory responses, and pathological autonomic nervous system remodeling [ 30 ]. According to the 2024 ESC guidelines, catheter ablation is recommended as the first-line treatment for patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, advocating PVI alone, and for patients with symptomatic persistent AF refractory to antiarrhythmic drug (AAD) therapy, minimally invasive thoracoscopic ablation or hybrid ablation procedures should be considered to prevent AF-related symptoms, recurrence, and disease progression (Class of Recommendation IIa, Level of Evidence A) [ 3 ]. However, for persistent atrial fibrillation, the superiority of ablation over pharmacological therapy remains unclear, and the optimal ablation strategy has yet to be definitively established. In addition, some studies such as Shinsuke Miyazaki et al. [ 31 ] performed additional ablation of the left roof line in addition to CB for PVI. Patients with persistent AF who underwent complete roof line modification demonstrated a significantly higher rate of freedom from ATA recurrence compared to those without comprehensive roof ablation (94.4% vs. 75.0%, p = 0.0049). Although more extensive ablation strategies beyond PVI have been advocated clinically for persistent AF, no conclusive evidence has established that additional extra-PV ablation approaches further improve procedural success rates [ 14 ]. This conclusion aligns with the results derived from our subgroup analysis. Future studies should prioritize investigating the most efficacious ablation strategy for persistent AF, particularly through rigorous comparison of lesion sets and verification of substrate-specific targets. Among the included articles, only the study by Akkaya et al. was based on patients with persistent atrial fibrillation and left atrial enlargement. The study still found that among patients with single pulmonary vein isolation without roof lines (RLs), the midterm survival rate without AF/ LA tachycardia (LAT) was comparable between the CB group and the RF group. However, for patients who received additional RLs, the survival rate without AF/LAT was lower in the RF group than in the CB group. Therefore, RL creation during CB can be a viable alternative to RF for patients with persistent atrial fibrillation and left atrial enlargement. Procedure and fluoroscopy time In terms of safety, it can be observed that the total procedural time of CB is significantly shorter than that of RF. Among the 8 literatures that included the study of operative time, significant heterogeneity can be observed, which may be caused by differences in countries, patients' basic conditions, surgeons' proficiency, and implemented intervention measures. However, this does not affect the results we obtained, and the final results of all studies are consistent with ours. In terms of fluoroscopy time, there is no significant difference between the two groups. However, there is also large heterogeneity among the related studies. The sources of heterogeneity may be related to national differences, different patient ethnic groups, anatomical variations, surgeons' proficiency, and different intervention measures. This phenomenon may be attributed to several factors: (1) The proficiency of the operator; (2) preferential use of RF ablation in cases with anatomically complex substrates requiring extended fluoroscopic verification; and (3) heterogeneity in 3D electroanatomical mapping system utilization (e.g., Carto3 vs. EnSite Precision), which differentially impacts fluoroscopy reduction potential. safety Regarding complications in this meta-analysis, only PNP shows a statistical difference between the CB group and the RF group, with a higher incidence in the CB group. This result is consistent with that of paroxysmal AF. PNP is the most commonly observed complication of CB ablation, with an incidence of approximately 6% (ranging from 3 to 11%) in clinical surgeries [ 32 – 34 ], mainly related to its anatomical structure. The right phrenic nerve is short in distance from the right inferior pulmonary vein and the right superior pulmonary vein, especially the shortest distance from the right superior pulmonary vein is about 2.1 mm [ 35 ]. Therefore, the phrenic nerve is more likely to be damaged during CB ablation in the right superior pulmonary vein. In the early STOP AF study [ 36 ], the incidence of PNP in CB ablation was approximately 11.2%. Fortunately, most patients' symptoms were temporary, and only about 1.5% of patients still had persistent PNP symptoms after one year. For this common complication, surgeons will conduct certain computed tomographic (CT) examinations before the operation to evaluate the anatomical structure of the left atrium and pulmonary veins. During the operation, the pacing electrode is placed in the superior vena cava above the cryoballoon for pacing, or the pacing electrode is placed in the right subclavian vein for stable pacing. At the same time, the surgeon manually presses under the xiphoid process to feel the diaphragmatic pulsation. If the occurrence of PNP is observed during the operation, the operation should be stopped immediately to allow the tissue to rewarm as soon as possible to prevent further aggravation of the damage. Moreover, compared with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, the incidence of PNP in persistent atrial fibrillation is higher. The reason may be that in addition to pulmonary veins, a larger-scale ablation may be required for persistent atrial fibrillation. Currently, most of the cryoballoons commonly used in our clinical practice are second-generation CB. Among the literatures we included, only the studies by Boveda et al. and Hoffman et al. used the first-generation CB. The study by Furrnkranz et al. [ 37 ] concluded that compared with the first-generation balloon, the second-generation CB significantly improves the success rate of pulmonary vein isolation, reduces the operative time and fluoroscopy time, and some subsequent prospective studies have confirmed this. However, the second-generation CB increases the incidence of PNP while enhancing the cryo efficacy. Therefore, more stringent monitoring of diaphragmatic movement is required during the operation. Limitations Our study has several limitations. Significant heterogeneity was observed in key outcomes, particularly procedural and fluoroscopy times. Potential sources of heterogeneity include operator experience, variations in surgical interventions, ablation scope, and whether additional ablation strategies beyond PVI were performed. Subgroup analysis of the efficacy of RF ablation strategies revealed no statistically significant differences. However, these findings require cautious interpretation due to uneven covariate distribution and limited sample size in each subgroup. The predominance of observational studies in our analysis introduces inherent methodological constraints. Certain studies employed non-randomized allocation of ablation modalities, as evidenced by the exclusion of CB ablation in patients presenting with severe left atrial wall thinning or pulmonary venous anatomical anomalies [ 16 ]. Procedural variability was further compounded by operator decisions to perform additional ablation targets (LA roof, posterior wall, mitral isthmus, or complex fractionated atrial electrograms) based on individual intraoperative findings, leading to baseline characteristic disparities between groups that increase susceptibility to selection bias and indication confounding. Follow-up duration discrepancies (12–24 months) across studies and inconsistent use of implantable monitoring devices for asymptomatic atrial fibrillation detection introduced outcome definition variability. In the subsequent follow-up, only a few studies used implantable devices for monitoring, which led to missed detections of asymptomatic atrial fibrillation recurrence and variations in outcome definitions. Current evidence from most studies confirms substantial differences in arrhythmia detection rates among various post-ablation monitoring strategies, with implantable cardiac monitors (ICMs) established as the gold standard [ 38 ]. The CRYSTAL-AF trial by Healey et al. [ 39 ] demonstrated that implantable cardiac monitors (ILRs/CIEDs) achieved an 8- to tenfold higher detection rate of occult atrial fibrillation compared to conventional monitoring strategies (29.3% vs. 3.0% over 12 months, HR = 8.8, 95% CI 4.2–18.4, P < 0.001). In subgroup analyses stratified by different post-ablation monitoring modalities, our findings demonstrate significant discrepancies compared to prior studies. This discrepancy may stem from limited sample sizes within subgroups (high-sensitivity: n = 3 studies; low-sensitivity: n = 5 studies), resulting in insufficient statistical power to detect true heterogeneity. We acknowledge this as a methodological limitation and advocate for standardized monitoring protocols in future studies to mitigate surveillance bias. These critical confounding factors were not quantitatively analyzed in our current study and require further validation through prospective investigations with standardized protocols. Conclusions CB can be used as an alternative therapy to RF for persAF, both of which have considerable efficacy and safety. No significant differences were observed between CB and RF ablation in terms of freedom from ATA recurrence or fluoroscopy time. However, CB can significantly reduce total procedural time with the probability of high PNP. Supplementary Information Additional file 1. documents.title: Comparison between clopidogrel and ticagrelor in CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles coronary artery disease and stroke patients: a meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: It is suggested that in patients with coronary artery diseases (CAD) and stroke, the use of ticagrelor and aspirin may perform better than clopidogrel and aspirin regarding the risk of thrombosis/embolism, including recurrent myocardial infarction (MI) and cardiovascular death, especially in those carrying CYP2C19 loss-of-function (LOF) alleles. Therefore, we conducted the present systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate the effect of clopidogrel and ticagrelor in CAD and stroke patients with CYP2C19 LOF alleles (poor metabolizers of clopidogrel).
METHODS: We performed the current systematic review and meta-analysis by searching for all eligible publications on PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to November 2024. A search strategy employing three primary keywords in conjunction with their corresponding Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms: "Ticagrelor" AND "Clopidogrel" AND "CYP2C19" (PROSPERO ID CRD420251050533). We implemented the odds ratio (OR) as an effect estimate for the dichotomous variables. The analysis was done at 95% confidence intervals (CI), and the p-value was significant if it was less than or equal to 0.05.
RESULTS: Using clopidogrel was associated with an increased risk of thrombosis/embolism compared with ticagrelor, showing OR = 1.78 (95%CI, 1.08, 2.95; p = 0.02). Also, clopidogrel led to an increased risk of stroke, whether when used in stroke or CAD patients with CYP2C19 LOF alleles, compared with ticagrelor, with an overall OR = 1.43 (95%CI, 1.23, 1.66; p 2 = 88%, p < 0.00001.
CONCLUSION: The meta-analysis of the selected articles indicated a preference for ticagrelor over clopidogrel in patients with stroke or CAD possessing CYP2C19 LOF alleles. The reduced incidence of thrombosis/embolism and associated events, such as stroke and MI, was noted in individuals administered ticagrelor in comparison to those receiving clopidogrel. Bleeding remains a concern with ticagrelor; however, current studies indicate its safety since there are no significant changes in the risk of minor and major bleeding and ICH compared to clopidogrel.

Abstract Background It is suggested that in patients with coronary artery diseases (CAD) and stroke, the use of ticagrelor and aspirin may perform better than clopidogrel and aspirin regarding the risk of thrombosis/embolism, including recurrent myocardial infarction (MI) and cardiovascular death, especially in those carrying CYP 2 C19 loss-of-function (LOF) alleles. Therefore, we conducted the present systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate the effect of clopidogrel and ticagrelor in CAD and stroke patients with CYP 2 C19 LOF alleles (poor metabolizers of clopidogrel). Methods We performed the current systematic review and meta-analysis by searching for all eligible publications on PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to November 2024. A search strategy employing three primary keywords in conjunction with their corresponding Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms: “Ticagrelor” AND “Clopidogrel” AND “CYP2C19” (PROSPERO ID CRD420251050533). We implemented the odds ratio (OR) as an effect estimate for the dichotomous variables. The analysis was done at 95% confidence intervals (CI), and the p -value was significant if it was less than or equal to 0.05. Results Using clopidogrel was associated with an increased risk of thrombosis/embolism compared with ticagrelor, showing OR = 1.78 (95%CI, 1.08, 2.95; p = 0.02). Also, clopidogrel led to an increased risk of stroke, whether when used in stroke or CAD patients with CYP 2 C19 LOF alleles, compared with ticagrelor, with an overall OR = 1.43 (95%CI, 1.23, 1.66; p < 0.00001) and a higher rate of MI with OR = 1.53 (95%CI, 1.22, 1.92; p = 0.0003). No significant difference was observed between the two groups (clopidogrel and ticagrelor) in stroke or CAD patients with OR = 0.98 (95%CI, 0.79, 1.22; p = 0.87). Also, no significant difference was observed between both groups regarding the risk of minor bleeding in stroke or CAD patients with OR = 0.66 (95%CI, 0.42, 1.05; p = 0.08) and any types of bleeding (major or minor bleeding) with overall OR = 0.81 (95%CI, 0.54, 1.21; p = 0.3) and I 2 = 88%, p < 0.00001. Conclusion The meta-analysis of the selected articles indicated a preference for ticagrelor over clopidogrel in patients with stroke or CAD possessing CYP 2 C19 LOF alleles. The reduced incidence of thrombosis/embolism and associated events, such as stroke and MI, was noted in individuals administered ticagrelor in comparison to those receiving clopidogrel. Bleeding remains a concern with ticagrelor; however, current studies indicate its safety since there are no significant changes in the risk of minor and major bleeding and ICH compared to clopidogrel.
